summary: The domestic apple descends mainly from the wild apple forests of the Tian Shan mountains of Kazakhstan, carried west and east along the Silk Road. Apples do not come true from seed, so every named variety — from 'Gala' to 'Bramley' — is a clone propagated by grafting, some for centuries.
nativeRange: Domesticated from Malus sieversii of Central Asia (Tian Shan), with genes from M. sylvestris; cultivated throughout temperate regions worldwide
abilities: Self-incompatible: most varieties need pollen from a different variety to set fruit
Seeds are genetically shuffled, so almost every pip grows into a new, unique apple
Requires winter chilling (often 500–1,000 hours below 7 °C) to break dormancy and flower well
Fruit stores for months in cool conditions as cells slowly respire sugars
edibleParts: fruit (raw, cooked, juiced, fermented to cider)
edibilityNote: Flesh and skin are wholesome. Seeds contain amygdalin, which releases cyanide when chewed; a few swallowed whole are harmless, but large quantities of crushed seeds should be avoided.

uses.use: Grated raw apple (rich in pectin) given for diarrhoea; stewed apple for convalescents
Apple preparations (e.g. murabba-e-seb) used as a heart and brain tonic

medicinal.cautions: Seeds contain amygdalin (cyanogenic). Apple allergy (cross-reacting with birch pollen) causes oral itching in some people.

fruit.season: Late summer to late autumn (Northern Hemisphere)
fruit.description: Round to conical fruit 5–10 cm across, skin green, yellow or red, crisp white to cream flesh around a papery five-chambered core; the swollen fleshy part develops from the floral receptacle, not the ovary.

seed.description: Glossy dark-brown to almost black teardrop-shaped pips, flattened, about 7–10 mm long, typically 1–2 in each of the five core chambers
seed.dispersal: Animals (deer, bears, birds, horses) eat the fruit and pass the seeds
seed.germination: Needs 60–90 days of moist cold stratification at 1–5 °C; seedlings will not resemble the parent

grow.zones: USDA 3–8 (varies by cultivar; some low-chill types to 9–10)
grow.water: Moderate; regular water while fruit swells
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained loam, pH 6–7; avoid waterlogged ground
grow.propagation: Grafting or budding of named cultivars onto rootstocks (e.g. M9 dwarf, MM106 semi-vigorous); seed only for breeding or rootstocks
grow.timeToHarvest: 2–4 years on dwarfing rootstock; 5–8 years on vigorous stock
steps: Buy a grafted tree of a variety suited to your chill hours, and plant a second compatible variety (or a crab apple) nearby for cross-pollination.
Plant bare-root in winter with the graft union 5–10 cm above soil; stake dwarf rootstocks permanently.
Water deeply weekly in the first two summers and mulch a 1 m circle to suppress grass.
Prune in winter to an open-centre or central-leader shape, removing crossing, diseased and inward-growing wood; thin fruitlets to one per cluster in early summer.
Pick when the fruit lifts and twists off easily and pips have turned brown.

lore: In Norse myth the goddess Iðunn kept apples that preserved the youth of the gods, and in Greek myth Eris's golden apple 'for the fairest' sparked the Trojan War. Johnny Appleseed (John Chapman) planted seedling nurseries across the American frontier in the early 1800s, mostly for cider.
funFact: An apple grown from a seed is almost never like its parent — the 'Granny Smith' itself arose as a chance seedling in Australia in 1868.

summary: Domesticated in South Asia over 4,000 years ago, the mango is the national fruit of India, Pakistan and the Philippines. A long-lived evergreen that can exceed 30 m, it bears hundreds of fruit a year and some trees are known to fruit for over 300 years.
nativeRange: Indo-Burma region: north-east India, Bangladesh, Myanmar; cultivated throughout the tropics and subtropics
abilities: Polyembryonic varieties produce several seedlings from one seed, most of them genetic clones of the mother tree
Flowers in huge panicles of up to several thousand tiny blossoms, pollinated mainly by flies
Deep taproot lets mature trees survive long dry seasons
Sap contains urushiol-like resorcinols, related to the irritant in poison ivy
edibleParts: young leaves (cooked, in parts of Southeast Asia)
edibilityNote: Ripe flesh is safe. Skin and sap contain urushiol-related compounds that cause contact dermatitis around the mouth in sensitive people, especially those allergic to poison ivy or cashew. Burning mango wood releases irritant smoke.

uses.use: Bark, leaves and seed kernel used as astringents for diarrhoea and bleeding; unripe fruit drink (aam panna) against heatstroke
Stem-bark extract (Vimang) developed as an antioxidant supplement

medicinal.cautions: Sap and peel can cause dermatitis; cross-reactivity with cashew, pistachio and poison ivy.

fruit.season: Spring to summer (March–August in South Asia)
fruit.description: Oval to kidney-shaped drupe 5–25 cm long, green ripening to yellow, orange or red-blushed; juicy, fragrant orange flesh around a large fibrous stone.

seed.description: Single large flattened oval seed enclosed in a hard, fibrous, hairy whitish husk (the stone); the kernel inside is kidney-shaped, cream to pale brown, 4–7 cm long
seed.dispersal: Large mammals (bats, monkeys, elephants) and humans; seeds are recalcitrant and die if dried
seed.germination: Sow fresh within days of eating; remove husk and plant kernel 2–3 cm deep, hump up; sprouts in 2–4 weeks at 25–30 °C

grow.water: Moderate; a dry season before flowering improves fruit set
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained; tolerates sandy and lateritic soils, pH 5.5–7.5
grow.propagation: Veneer or cleft grafting onto seedling rootstock; polyembryonic seed comes true
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years from graft; 6–10 years from seed; fruit ripens 100–150 days after flowering
steps: Choose a grafted tree of a variety suited to your climate (e.g. 'Kent' or 'Nam Doc Mai' for humid areas resistant to anthracnose).
Plant in the warmest, sunniest spot available, at least 8 m from buildings; do not amend the planting hole heavily.
Water regularly for the first two years, then reduce watering in the 2–3 months before flowering to induce bloom.
Prune after harvest to keep the canopy open and low (3–4 m) for easier picking and less fungal disease.
Pick when the shoulders fill out and the flesh near the stem yields slightly; ripen at room temperature.

lore: Mughal emperor Akbar planted the Lakhi Bagh, an orchard of 100,000 mango trees near Darbhanga, and the Buddha is said to have rested in a mango grove gifted by the courtesan Amrapali. In Hindu tradition mango leaves are strung over doorways (toran) at festivals and weddings.
funFact: Mango, cashew and pistachio are botanical cousins — and all three are relatives of poison ivy.

summary: The banana plant is not a tree but the world's largest herb: its 'trunk' is a pseudostem of tightly rolled leaf sheaths. Wild Musa acuminata has fruit packed with hard seeds; the seedless sterile triploids we eat, like the 'Cavendish', are propagated only as clones.
nativeRange: Southeast Asia and Malesia to northern Australia; cultivated throughout the tropics
abilities: Pseudostem can grow to about 3–7 m in under a year, then dies after fruiting while suckers replace it
Cultivated triploids set fruit without pollination (parthenocarpy)
Wild forms are pollinated at night by bats and by day by sunbirds
Fruit curves upward as it grows, turning toward light (negative geotropism)
edibleParts: leaves used as food wrappers and plates
edibilityNote: Fruit, flower and stem core are all eaten. Wild seeded bananas have large hard seeds that must be spat out.

uses.use: Unripe banana and banana-stem juice used for diarrhoea and urinary stones
BRAT diet (bananas, rice, applesauce, toast) for recovery from gastroenteritis
Sap applied to wounds and burns

medicinal.cautions: Latex-fruit syndrome: people with latex allergy may react to banana.

fruit.description: Elongated curved berry 10–30 cm, borne in 'hands' on a hanging bunch; green ripening to yellow, flesh cream and starchy-sweet. Cultivated forms show only tiny black specks where seeds aborted.

seed.description: In wild plants: hard, angular, black or dark-brown seeds about 4–6 mm, densely packed in the flesh. Cultivated dessert bananas show only rows of tiny brown-black specks of aborted ovules
seed.dispersal: Bats, birds and primates (wild); vegetatively by suckers (cultivated)
seed.germination: Wild seed: scarify and soak, sow warm (25–30 °C); erratic, 2 weeks to several months

grow.sun: Full sun; shelter from wind which shreds leaves
grow.water: High; constant moisture
grow.soil: Rich, deep, well-drained loam high in organic matter, pH 5.5–7
grow.propagation: Suckers (sword suckers with narrow leaves are best), corms, or tissue-cultured plantlets
grow.timeToHarvest: 9–15 months from planting to bunch; fruit ready ~3 months after flowering
steps: Plant a sword sucker or tissue-culture plant in a hole enriched with compost, in a warm sheltered spot.
Feed heavily (bananas are hungry for potassium and nitrogen) and water deeply; mulch with chopped old leaves.
Keep one main stem plus one follower sucker per clump; cut away extra suckers.
After the last hand forms, snap off the male bud; harvest the bunch when fruits are plump and the first one yellows.
Cut down the spent pseudostem after harvest and chop it into mulch around the clump.

lore: Alexander the Great's soldiers reportedly saw sages resting under banana plants in the Indus valley, giving rise to Linnaeus's name Musa sapientum, 'fruit of the wise'. Bananas were among the first crops of New Guinea, where cultivation at Kuk Swamp dates back about 7,000 years.
funFact: Almost all export bananas are one clone, 'Cavendish', which replaced 'Gros Michel' after Panama disease wiped it out in the 1950s.

summary: One of the oldest cultivated fruit trees, grown in Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf for over 6,000 years. The date palm made oasis life possible across the Sahara and Arabia — its fruit a storable staple, its fronds and fibre a building material.
nativeRange: Probably the Persian Gulf region and south-west Asia; cultivated across North Africa, the Middle East, Pakistan and arid zones worldwide
abilities: Tolerates extreme heat (over 50 °C) and saline groundwater, provided roots reach water
Dioecious: separate male and female trees, traditionally hand-pollinated by climbing farmers
A 2,000-year-old seed from Masada germinated in 2005, among the oldest seeds ever germinated
A single female tree can produce 70–150 kg of fruit a year
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten fresh at the khalal (crunchy), rutab (soft) and tamr (dried) stages. Harvesting palm heart kills the tree.

uses.use: Ajwa dates eaten in the morning as protection; dates traditionally break the Ramadan fast
Dates as a strengthening food for the weak and during convalescence
Eaten in late pregnancy; some trials suggest it eases labour

medicinal.cautions: Very high in sugar; caution in diabetes.

fruit.description: Oblong fruit 3–7 cm long in heavy hanging clusters; green ripening to yellow or red, then brown and wrinkled when dried; sticky, sweet, honey-to-caramel flesh.

seed.description: Hard, elongated cylindrical seed, grey-brown, 2–3 cm long, with a deep groove along one side and a small dot-like germ pore on the back
seed.dispersal: Animals and humans; long viability in dry conditions
seed.germination: Soak 2–3 days, sow in warm moist sand at 25–35 °C; sprouts in 2–8 weeks. Half of seedlings will be male and fruit is variable

grow.water: Roots need deep water; leaves need dry heat. Low humidity at fruiting
grow.soil: Sandy, well-drained; tolerates salinity and alkalinity
grow.propagation: Offshoots (suckers) taken from the base of named female cultivars such as 'Medjool' or 'Deglet Noor'; tissue culture
grow.timeToHarvest: 4–7 years from offshoot; fruit ripens 150–200 days after pollination
steps: Detach an offshoot weighing 10–25 kg with roots from a female palm, or buy a tissue-cultured plant of a named variety.
Plant in full sun in deep sand, keeping the soil level at the offshoot's widest point; tie the fronds up to shade the heart while it roots.
Water deeply and often in the first year; mature palms need deep, infrequent irrigation.
In spring, place strands of male flowers inside opened female flower clusters (or dust with male pollen).
Thin bunches and bag them against birds and rain; harvest at the rutab or tamr stage.

lore: Mesopotamian tablets record date cultivation and hand-pollination as early as the 3rd millennium BCE, and Hammurabi's code fixed a fine for cutting down a tree in another man's orchard. The date palm is the most-mentioned fruit tree in the Qur'an, where Maryam is told to shake its trunk for ripe dates.
funFact: 'Methuselah', a palm sprouted in 2005 from a roughly 2,000-year-old seed found at Masada, has since fathered dates by pollinating 'Hannah', a female palm raised from another ancient seed.

summary: The fig may be the first plant humans domesticated: parthenocarpic figs found at Gilgal in the Jordan Valley date to about 11,400 years ago, before wheat. Its 'fruit' is actually an inverted flower cluster, a syconium, with hundreds of tiny flowers lining the inside.
nativeRange: South-west Asia and the eastern Mediterranean; widely cultivated in warm-temperate regions
abilities: Wild figs depend on a tiny wasp, Blastophaga psenes, which breeds inside the fig and pollinates it
Common figs (e.g. 'Brown Turkey') set fruit without pollination
Roots seek water aggressively and can crack walls and pipes
Thrives in poor, rocky, dry soil and grows out of cliff faces and ruins
edibleParts: leaves (as wrappers; used to infuse flavour)
edibilityNote: Fruit is safe. The milky latex of leaves and stems contains furanocoumarins that cause blistering burns when skin is exposed to sunlight (phytophotodermatitis).

uses.use: Dried figs as a laxative and for coughs and chest complaints
A poultice of figs laid on King Hezekiah's boil (2 Kings 20:7)
Fresh latex dabbed on warts

medicinal.cautions: Latex causes phytophotodermatitis and is a strong irritant; avoid latex in eyes. May contain natural rubber allergens.

fruit.season: Early summer (breba crop) and late summer to autumn (main crop)
fruit.description: Pear-shaped, 3–8 cm, skin green, purple or nearly black; inside, soft honey-sweet pink to red flesh packed with tiny crunchy achenes.

seed.description: Tiny, round to lens-shaped, yellow-tan 'seeds' (actually achenes), about 1–1.5 mm, hundreds per fig; in unpollinated common figs they are hollow and sterile
seed.germination: Only fertile (wasp-pollinated) seed sprouts; surface-sow on moist mix at 20–25 °C, 1–3 weeks

grow.zones: USDA 7–11 (to 6 with winter protection; dies back but resprouts)
grow.sun: Full sun, ideally against a warm wall
grow.water: Low–moderate once established; even moisture while fruit swells prevents splitting
grow.soil: Any well-drained soil, including poor, rocky, or chalky; pH 6–8
grow.propagation: Hardwood cuttings 20–30 cm taken in winter root very easily; also air layering and suckers
grow.timeToHarvest: 1–3 years from a rooted cutting
steps: Choose a self-fertile common fig variety (e.g. 'Brown Turkey', 'Chicago Hardy' for cold areas).
Plant against a sunny south- or west-facing wall; in rich soil, restrict roots in a box or large pot to encourage fruiting rather than leaves.
Water through dry summers once fruits form; avoid heavy nitrogen feeding.
In cold regions, wrap or mulch heavily in winter; prune in late winter to remove crowded and frost-damaged shoots.
Pick when figs droop on their stalks, soften and a drop of nectar appears at the eye; wear gloves against latex.

lore: In Genesis, Adam and Eve sew fig leaves to cover themselves, and Romulus and Remus were said to have been suckled by the she-wolf beneath the Ficus Ruminalis in Rome. The Buddha's Bodhi tree is a related fig, Ficus religiosa.
funFact: Gilgal figs, about 11,400 years old, came from a seedless mutant that could only survive by people planting cuttings — evidence of deliberate cultivation.

summary: A thorny, drought-hardy shrub or small tree whose leathery fruit holds hundreds of jewel-like seeds. Cultivated from Iran to the Mediterranean since the Bronze Age, it has symbolised fertility, abundance and resurrection in nearly every culture that grew it.
nativeRange: Iran to northern India (Caucasus, Persia, Afghanistan, Himalayan foothills); cultivated across the Mediterranean and arid subtropics
abilities: Tolerates drought, heat, alkaline and moderately saline soils
Fruit keeps for months on the shelf thanks to its tannin-rich leathery rind
Brilliant scarlet, trumpet-shaped flowers attract sunbirds and hummingbirds
Rind yields a yellow-brown dye used for Persian carpets and leather
edibilityNote: Arils and juice are eaten. Root and stem bark contain toxic alkaloids (pelletierines) and should not be consumed.

uses.use: Rind decoction for diarrhoea and dysentery; fruit as a heart tonic
Sour and sweet pomegranate juices prescribed to balance hot and cold temperaments
Root bark used to expel tapeworms

medicinal.cautions: Bark and root alkaloids are toxic. Juice may interact with some drugs metabolised by CYP enzymes (e.g. warfarin).

fruit.description: Round fruit 6–12 cm topped with a crown-like calyx; leathery red to yellow-pink rind enclosing white membranes and 200–1,400 juicy translucent arils, ruby to pale pink.

seed.description: Each seed is wrapped in a juicy, glassy red to pink aril; the seed itself is angular, cream to pale-yellow, woody, about 5–8 mm long
seed.germination: Clean off the aril, sow fresh 0.5 cm deep at 20–25 °C; sprouts in 2–6 weeks

grow.zones: USDA 7–11 (some Russian and Central Asian varieties to 6)
grow.water: Low–moderate; even watering at fruit set reduces splitting
grow.soil: Well-drained; tolerates poor, alkaline and loamy soils, pH 5.5–7.5
grow.propagation: Hardwood cuttings (25 cm, winter) root readily; seed for rootstock or novelty
grow.timeToHarvest: 2–3 years from cutting; fruit ripens 5–7 months after flowering
steps: Take 25 cm hardwood cuttings of a good variety (e.g. 'Wonderful', 'Bhagwa') in winter and root them in a pot or directly in the ground.
Plant in the hottest, sunniest place, training to a single trunk or a few stems; remove suckers from the base.
Water regularly in the first year, then deeply but infrequently; keep watering steady once fruit sets to avoid cracking.
Prune lightly in late winter, as fruit forms on short spurs on 2–3-year-old wood.
Harvest when the rind colours fully and the fruit sounds metallic when tapped; cut, don't pull.

lore: In Greek myth Persephone ate pomegranate seeds in the underworld, binding her there for part of each year and explaining the seasons. Pomegranates were embroidered on the hem of the Hebrew High Priest's robe and appear in the Qur'an as a fruit of paradise.
funFact: The city of Granada in Spain shares its name with the fruit, and the grenade was named after the pomegranate for its seed-like shrapnel.

summary: The defining tree of the Mediterranean, domesticated in the Levant around 7,000 years ago. Gnarled olive trees can live for well over 1,000 years, resprouting from their base after fire, frost or felling.
nativeRange: Mediterranean Basin and Near East (cultivated form); wild subspecies across Africa, Arabia and South Asia
abilities: Silvery leaves with scaly hairs reduce water loss, letting trees fruit on as little as 200–400 mm of rain
Resprouts from a burl (lignotuber) after the trunk is killed
Individual trees in Crete, Lebanon and Sardinia are estimated at 2,000–3,000 years old
Wind-pollinated; pollen is a major springtime allergen in the Mediterranean
edibilityNote: Raw olives are inedibly bitter because of oleuropein; they must be cured in brine, lye, water or dry salt before eating.

uses.use: Olive leaf tea for fever and high blood pressure
Olive oil eaten and applied to the body, called 'from a blessed tree'
Extra-virgin olive oil central to the Mediterranean diet; EU-authorised claim for polyphenols protecting blood lipids

medicinal.cautions: Leaf extracts may lower blood pressure and blood sugar; caution with antihypertensive and diabetes medication.

fruit.season: Autumn to winter (green olives October, black November–January)
fruit.description: Oval drupe 1–4 cm, green ripening through violet to black; oily, bitter flesh around a hard stone.

seed.description: A hard, pointed oval stone, pale brown and finely ridged, 1–2 cm long, enclosing a single slender cream-coloured seed
seed.dispersal: Birds (especially starlings and thrushes) and mammals
seed.germination: Slow and erratic: crack or clip the stone, cold-stratify 1–2 months, then sow warm; 1–3 months

grow.water: Low once established
grow.soil: Well-drained, even poor, stony or chalky; dislikes waterlogging, pH 6.5–8.5
grow.propagation: Semi-hardwood cuttings under mist, or grafting onto seedling or wild rootstock
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years for first crop; full production at 10–15 years
steps: Choose a cultivar suited to your climate and use (e.g. 'Arbequina' self-fertile for oil, 'Manzanilla' for table olives).
Plant in spring in a sunny, frost-sheltered spot with excellent drainage; on clay, plant on a mound.
Water weekly for the first summer, then only during long droughts; most olives fruit better with some summer water stress.
Prune in late winter to an open vase shape to let light into the canopy, since fruit forms on last year's growth.
Pick by hand or rake onto nets; cure table olives in brine (changed weekly) for 1–3 months, or press within 24 hours for oil.

lore: Athena won Athens from Poseidon by giving the city an olive tree, and olive wreaths crowned victors at the ancient Olympic Games. In Genesis the dove returns to Noah's ark with an olive leaf, the origin of the olive branch as a sign of peace.
funFact: Olive trees in the Garden of Gethsemane in Jerusalem have been radiocarbon-dated to the 12th century, and their roots may be far older.

summary: The Eurasian grape was domesticated in the South Caucasus and Near East around 8,000 years ago, where the oldest known wine residues were found in Georgian pottery. Thousands of cultivars, from 'Cabernet Sauvignon' to 'Thompson Seedless', are clones propagated by cuttings.
nativeRange: Wild subspecies sylvestris from Western Europe to the Caucasus and Central Asia; cultivated worldwide in temperate and Mediterranean climates
abilities: Climbs using coiling tendrils that wrap around supports within hours of touching them
Domestication turned a dioecious wild vine into self-pollinating hermaphrodite cultivars
Fruit skin hosts wild yeasts that can ferment crushed grapes into wine unaided
Can live and fruit for centuries; a vine in Maribor, Slovenia, is over 400 years old
edibleParts: fruit (fresh, dried as raisins, juiced, fermented)
edibilityNote: Fruit and leaves are eaten widely. Grapes and raisins are toxic to dogs and can cause kidney failure.

uses.use: Drākṣā (raisins) as a cooling laxative and in tonics such as Drākṣārishta
Red vine leaf extract for chronic venous insufficiency (heavy, swollen legs)
Raisins (munaqqa) for coughs and as a nutritive

medicinal.cautions: Grapes and raisins are toxic to dogs and cats. Alcohol from wine carries its own risks.

fruit.description: Round to oval berries 1–3 cm in tight bunches; skin green, golden, red, purple or blue-black with a waxy bloom; juicy translucent flesh.

seed.description: Pear- or teardrop-shaped pips with a short beak, light to dark brown, 4–7 mm long, with a hard woody coat; usually 1–4 per berry (absent or vestigial in seedless types)
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 2–3 months at 2–4 °C, then sow at 20–25 °C; 2–8 weeks. Offspring differ from the parent

grow.zones: USDA 6–10 (vinifera); hybrids and American species to 4
grow.water: Low–moderate; mild water stress after fruit set improves flavour
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained, even stony or poor; pH 5.5–7.5
grow.propagation: Hardwood cuttings of 3–4 buds taken in winter; grafting onto phylloxera-resistant rootstock where the pest is present
grow.timeToHarvest: First crop in year 2–3; full crop by year 4–5
steps: Select a variety for your heat and season length; where phylloxera or nematodes occur, buy vines grafted onto resistant American rootstock.
Plant in winter or early spring beside a sturdy trellis, wire fence or pergola, 1.5–2.5 m apart.
In year one, let one strong shoot grow and tie it up as the trunk; remove others.
Each winter, prune hard — leave 2-bud spurs (spur pruning) or 1–2 long canes (cane pruning), since fruit forms on new shoots from last year's wood.
Thin leaves around bunches for airflow, net against birds, and pick when berries taste sweet and seeds have turned brown.

lore: Clay jars at Gadachrili Gora in Georgia hold wine residues from about 6000 BCE, and wine was central to the rites of Dionysus and the Christian Eucharist. Persian poets such as Omar Khayyam and Hafez made the vine and its wine a symbol of mystical intoxication.
funFact: Nearly every European wine vine today grows on American rootstock, after the aphid-like phylloxera devastated Europe's vineyards in the 1860s–1890s.

summary: The sweet orange is an ancient hybrid of pomelo and mandarin that arose in southern China; iNaturalist now groups it with bitter and other oranges under Citrus × aurantium. It is the world's most-grown citrus, its highly scented blossom (orange blossom, neroli) as valued as its fruit.
nativeRange: Hybrid origin in southern China and north-east India; cultivated throughout the tropics, subtropics and Mediterranean
abilities: Many seeds are polyembryonic and produce clones of the mother tree via nucellar embryos
Peel is studded with oil glands full of limonene, which repels many insects
Fruit can hang ripe on the tree for months without spoiling, 'storing' itself
Blossom nectar yields a prized single-flower honey
edibilityNote: Fruit, juice, peel and blossom water are widely eaten. Essential oil is concentrated and not for internal use.

uses.use: Dried citrus peel (chén pí, mainly of mandarin) to regulate qi, aid digestion and resolve phlegm
Oranges and lemons as a cure for scurvy, shown in James Lind's 1747 trial
Orange-blossom water as a calming tonic

medicinal.cautions: Peel oil is phototoxic on skin in sunlight. Bitter-orange types (same species in iNaturalist) contain synephrine, a stimulant to avoid with heart conditions.

fruit.season: Winter to spring (Northern Hemisphere); 'Valencia' into summer
fruit.description: Round fruit 6–10 cm, with an oil-dotted orange rind, a white spongy pith (albedo) and 10–13 juicy segments filled with tiny juice vesicles.

seed.description: Pale cream to whitish, ovoid to wedge-shaped seeds with a pointed end and wrinkled surface, about 8–12 mm long; seedless navel and 'Valencia' types have few or none
seed.germination: Sow fresh, never dried, 1 cm deep at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 2–4 weeks. Often several shoots per seed

grow.water: Moderate; deep regular watering, never waterlogged
grow.soil: Sandy loam, well-drained, pH 6–7.5
grow.propagation: Budding onto rootstocks such as trifoliate orange or 'Carrizo' citrange; seed for rootstocks
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–4 years from a budded tree; fruit takes 7–12 months from flower to ripe
steps: Buy a budded tree on a rootstock suited to your soil and cold (trifoliate for cold, 'Swingle' for sandy soils).
Plant with the bud union well above soil in full sun, sheltered from cold wind; in pots use a fast-draining citrus mix.
Water deeply when the top 5 cm of soil is dry; feed with a citrus fertiliser containing iron, zinc and manganese in spring and summer.
Remove any shoots from the rootstock below the graft; prune only to shape and remove dead wood.
Taste-test before picking — colour is not a reliable sign of ripeness, and fruit stores well on the tree.

lore: Portuguese traders brought improved sweet oranges from Asia in the 16th century, which is why the fruit is called 'portokali' in Greek and 'burtuqāl' in Arabic. The Versailles orangery built for Louis XIV still houses over 1,000 potted citrus and other trees, wheeled outside each summer.
funFact: In tropical climates without cool nights, ripe oranges stay green outside — the orange colour develops only when temperatures drop.

summary: The lemon is a hybrid of citron and bitter orange that arose in north-east India or Burma and travelled west with Arab traders. Unlike most citrus, it flowers and fruits almost year-round, carrying blossom and ripe fruit at once.
nativeRange: Hybrid origin in north-east India, northern Myanmar or south China; cultivated in the subtropics and Mediterranean worldwide
abilities: Flowers repeatedly through the year ('everbearing') in mild climates
Juice is about 5–6% citric acid, with a pH near 2.2
Peel oil glands release limonene and citral, deterring insects
Thorny shoots protect young growth from browsing
edibleParts: zest and peel (fresh, candied, preserved in salt)
edibilityNote: Juice and peel are widely used. The acid erodes tooth enamel with frequent neat use.

uses.use: Lemon juice issued to sailors against scurvy from 1795
Nimbu with warm water and salt as a digestive and for nausea
Hot lemon and honey for colds and sore throats

medicinal.cautions: Peel oil is phototoxic on skin exposed to sun. Acid can aggravate reflux and erode teeth.

fruit.description: Oval fruit 7–12 cm with a nipple-like tip; bright yellow, oil-dotted rind and pale-yellow, very sour segments.

seed.description: Smooth, pale cream to whitish, pointed-oval seeds about 8–10 mm long, slightly flattened
seed.germination: Sow fresh 1 cm deep at 22–28 °C; sprouts in 2–3 weeks. Seedlings take 5–10 years to fruit

grow.water: Moderate; keep evenly moist, never soggy
grow.soil: Well-drained loam or sandy soil, pH 5.5–7
grow.propagation: Budding or grafting onto rootstock; lemons also root from semi-hardwood cuttings
grow.timeToHarvest: 2–3 years from a grafted tree; fruit 6–9 months from flower
steps: Choose a variety for your climate: 'Eureka' or 'Lisbon' for warm zones, 'Meyer' for pots and cooler areas.
Plant in full sun in very well-drained soil; in pots, use a 40–50 cm container with gritty mix and move indoors below 0 °C.
Water when the top few cm dry out and feed monthly in the growing season with a citrus fertiliser.
Pinch out water shoots and rootstock suckers; prune lightly after the main harvest.
Pick when fully yellow and slightly glossy; lemons store on the tree for weeks.

lore: Arab agronomists such as Ibn al-Awwam described lemon cultivation in Andalusia in the 12th century, and Genoese ships carried lemons across the Mediterranean. Preserved lemons remain a cornerstone of Moroccan cuisine.
funFact: A 1747 experiment by naval surgeon James Lind, giving scurvy-stricken sailors oranges and lemons, is often called one of the first controlled clinical trials.

summary: A small understorey tree of the Amazon whose seeds become chocolate. Its tiny flowers sprout directly from the trunk and are pollinated almost entirely by minute midges, and Mesoamerican peoples prized its beans so highly they used them as money.
nativeRange: Upper Amazon basin (Ecuador, Peru, Colombia, Brazil); domesticated in Mesoamerica and South America; grown across the humid tropics
abilities: Cauliflorous: flowers and pods grow straight from the trunk and old branches
Pollinated by biting midges (Forcipomyia) only a few millimetres long
Thrives in deep shade beneath taller rainforest trees
Seeds contain theobromine, a stimulant toxic to dogs
edibleParts: seeds (fermented, dried and roasted for cocoa and chocolate)
edibilityNote: Beans and the sweet white pulp are safe for people. Theobromine makes chocolate dangerous to dogs, cats and horses.

uses.use: Cacao drinks mixed with herbs for fatigue, fever and digestive complaints, recorded in the Florentine Codex
Cocoa flavanols studied for improving blood-vessel function and lowering blood pressure

medicinal.cautions: Toxic to dogs and cats. Stimulant effects can cause palpitations or migraine in sensitive people.

fruit.description: Ridged, rugby-ball-shaped pod 15–30 cm long, green or red maturing to yellow, orange or purple, with a thick husk around 20–60 seeds in sweet-tart white pulp.

seed.description: Almond-shaped, flattened oval beans 2–3 cm long, purple to ivory-white inside (white in rare criollo types), coated in slippery white pulp
seed.dispersal: Monkeys, squirrels and bats crack pods to eat the pulp and discard seeds
seed.germination: Recalcitrant: sow within a week of opening the pod, 1 cm deep, at 25–30 °C in humid shade; sprouts in 1–2 weeks

grow.sun: Partial shade (30–50%); young plants need shade
grow.water: High; 1,500–2,500 mm rain evenly spread
grow.soil: Deep, humus-rich, well-drained, pH 5–7.5
grow.propagation: Seed, or grafting / rooted cuttings of selected clones
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years to first pods; pods ripen 5–6 months after pollination
steps: Sow fresh seed in deep bags under shade, or buy grafted plants of a productive, disease-tolerant clone.
Plant out under temporary shade (banana, plantain) and permanent shade trees (e.g. Gliricidia, Inga) about 3 m apart.
Mulch heavily with leaf litter, which also breeds the pollinating midges; keep soil moist.
Prune to a single trunk with a 'jorquette' of 3–5 main branches and remove diseased pods promptly against black pod and frosty pod rot.
Cut ripe pods with a knife, scoop beans and pulp, ferment in covered heaps or boxes for 5–7 days, then sun-dry before roasting.

lore: Residues on pottery at Santa Ana-La Florida in Ecuador show cacao was used about 5,300 years ago, and the Aztec emperor Moctezuma II is said to have drunk chocolate from golden cups. Linnaeus named the genus Theobroma, 'food of the gods'.
funFact: In the Aztec market, a turkey hen cost about 100 cacao beans and a tomato one bean — and counterfeiters filled empty bean husks with mud.

summary: An evergreen shrub of Ethiopia's highland forests whose roasted seeds make about 60% of the world's coffee. A natural hybrid of two wild species, it is unusual in its genus for being self-fertile, and wild populations are Endangered by deforestation and climate change.
nativeRange: South-western Ethiopia, the Boma Plateau of South Sudan and Mount Marsabit in Kenya; cultivated in tropical highlands worldwide
abilities: Allotetraploid hybrid of Coffea canephora and Coffea eugenioides
Self-pollinating, unlike almost all other Coffea species
Caffeine in seeds and leaves deters insects and inhibits competing seedlings
Jasmine-scented white flowers open all at once after the first rains
edibleParts: leaves (brewed as tea in Ethiopia and Sumatra)
edibilityNote: Beans, cherry husk and leaves are used for drinks. Caffeine overdose from concentrated products can be dangerous.

uses.use: Coffee drunk to stay awake during night prayers in the 15th century
Caffeine is an approved drug, used with analgesics for headache and for apnoea in premature infants
Coffee leaves and husks brewed with butter or salt as a tonic

medicinal.cautions: Caffeine can cause insomnia, anxiety and palpitations; limit in pregnancy. Unfiltered coffee raises LDL cholesterol via cafestol.

fruit.season: Varies by region; 6–9 months after flowering
fruit.description: Oval cherry 1–1.5 cm, green ripening to bright red or yellow, with thin sweet pulp around two seeds back to back.

seed.description: Pale greenish-grey to bluish 'green beans', oval, about 1 cm long, flat on one face with a central S-shaped groove, domed on the other; covered by a papery parchment and a silver skin. A single round seed ('peaberry') forms in some cherries
seed.dispersal: Birds and mammals eat the cherries
seed.germination: Remove pulp, sow fresh seed in parchment 1 cm deep at 25–30 °C in shade; slow, 6–10 weeks

grow.zones: USDA 10–12; best in frost-free tropical highlands (900–2,000 m)
grow.sun: Partial shade; tolerates sun with ample water
grow.water: Moderate–high, with a short dry season to trigger flowering
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5–6.5), rich volcanic or forest loam
grow.propagation: Seed (comes reasonably true because self-pollinating); cuttings of selected lines
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–4 years to first crop
steps: Sow fresh seed of a named variety (e.g. 'Typica', 'Bourbon', or rust-resistant 'Castillo') in shaded nursery bags.
Transplant at 6–12 months, 2–2.5 m apart, under light shade trees that also protect against wind.
Mulch, feed with compost, and water during dry spells, while allowing a short dry spell before the main rains to induce mass flowering.
Prune to control height (1.5–2 m) and remove old unproductive stems periodically; watch for coffee leaf rust.
Hand-pick only fully red cherries; process by washing and fermenting or by sun-drying whole cherries.

lore: Ethiopian legend credits the goatherd Kaldi with noticing his goats dancing after eating coffee cherries. Coffee houses spread from Yemen to Mecca, Cairo and Istanbul by the 16th century, and Ottoman authorities repeatedly tried to ban them as places of sedition.
funFact: The Typica coffee of much of the Caribbean and Latin America traces to a few plants: one given to Louis XIV in 1714 was the source of seedlings Gabriel de Clieu carried to Martinique around 1720, sharing his water ration with it on the voyage.

summary: An evergreen camellia whose young leaves give every true tea — white, green, oolong, black and pu-erh differ only in processing. Left unpruned it becomes a tree; some Assam-type trees in Yunnan are claimed to exceed 1,000 years old.
nativeRange: South-west China (Yunnan) and adjacent northern Myanmar, Laos and north-east India; cultivated in Asia, East Africa and South America
abilities: Accumulates fluoride and aluminium from acid soils in its leaves
Contains L-theanine, an amino acid almost unique to tea, which smooths caffeine's effect
Can be repeatedly plucked: the bush regrows a fresh 'flush' every few weeks
Trees can live for many centuries
edibleParts: leaves (fermented and eaten as lahpet in Myanmar)
edibilityNote: Leaves are brewed or pickled. Very strong tea in excess can cause stomach upset and reduce iron absorption.

uses.use: Green tea to clear heat, refresh the mind and aid digestion; described in Lu Yu's Classic of Tea (c. 760 CE)
Eisai's 'Kissa Yōjōki' (1211) promoted tea for long life and wakefulness in meditation
Green-tea catechin ointment (sinecatechins) is a US FDA-approved drug for genital warts

medicinal.cautions: Caffeine; high-dose green-tea extract supplements have caused liver injury. Reduces absorption of non-haem iron.

fruit.description: Woody, round to three-lobed capsule 2–3 cm, green turning brown, splitting to release 1–3 seeds.

seed.description: Round to hemispherical, hard, smooth dark-brown seeds 1–1.5 cm across, oily inside
seed.dispersal: Gravity; rolled and cached by rodents
seed.germination: Short-lived: soak fresh seed 24 hours, discard floaters, sow 2–3 cm deep at 20–25 °C; 1–3 months

grow.sun: Partial shade to full sun in cooler areas
grow.water: Moderate–high; at least 1,200 mm rain or regular irrigation
grow.soil: Acidic (pH 4.5–6), well-drained, humus-rich
grow.propagation: Single-leaf cuttings of selected clones, or seed
grow.timeToHarvest: 3 years before regular plucking
steps: Plant a rooted cutting in acidic, free-draining soil; in alkaline areas grow in a large pot of ericaceous compost.
Mulch with pine bark or leaf litter and water with rainwater if tap water is hard.
Prune back to about 75–100 cm in the second and third years to make a flat-topped, bushy 'plucking table'.
Pluck 'two leaves and a bud' from new flushes in spring and summer.
For green tea, steam or pan-fire leaves within hours, roll, and dry; for black tea, wither, roll to bruise, let oxidise 1–3 hours, then dry.

lore: Chinese legend says the emperor Shennong discovered tea in 2737 BCE when leaves blew into his boiling water. In 1848–51 the Scottish botanist Robert Fortune smuggled tea plants and seeds out of China for the East India Company, helping found the tea gardens of Darjeeling.
funFact: Almost every word for tea worldwide descends from either 'te' (via Dutch traders in Fujian, by sea) or 'cha' (by land along the Silk Road).

summary: A laurel-family tree from Mesoamerica whose oily fruit evolved, many think, to be swallowed whole by giant ground sloths and gomphotheres. Its flowers switch sex on a daily schedule to avoid self-pollination.
nativeRange: South-central Mexico to Guatemala and Central America; cultivated in tropical and Mediterranean climates worldwide
abilities: Synchronous dichogamy: 'A' and 'B' varieties open as female and male at opposite times of day
Fruit does not ripen on the tree; it softens only after picking
Flesh can be 15–30% oil, unusually high for a fruit
Leaves, bark and seed contain persin, a toxin dangerous to birds, horses and livestock
edibleParts: leaves (dried, as a flavouring in Mexican cooking — Mexican race only)
edibilityNote: The flesh is safe for people. Persin in leaves, skin, seed and bark is toxic to birds, rabbits, horses, goats and other livestock; the seed is not a food.

uses.use: Leaves and seed used in remedies for diarrhoea and as an aphrodisiac; recorded in the Florentine Codex
Avocado–soybean unsaponifiables (ASU) prescribed for osteoarthritis

medicinal.cautions: Leaves, skin and seed toxic to many animals. People with latex allergy may react (latex-fruit syndrome).

fruit.season: Varies by variety; often year-round in suitable climates
fruit.description: Pear-shaped to round fruit 7–20 cm, skin green to purple-black, smooth or pebbly ('Hass'); buttery pale-green to yellow flesh around one large seed.

seed.description: Large, round to egg-shaped seed 4–6 cm, with a thin papery brown seed coat over a hard cream-to-pinkish interior that browns when cut
seed.dispersal: Formerly megafauna; now humans and rodents
seed.germination: Clean seed, plant broad end down with the top exposed in moist mix (or suspend over water); roots in 2–6 weeks at 20–25 °C. Seedlings take 7–15 years to fruit and are unlike the parent

grow.zones: USDA 9b–11 (Mexican types to about −5 °C; West Indian to 0 °C)
grow.water: Moderate; regular deep watering, very sensitive to waterlogging
grow.soil: Very well-drained sandy loam, pH 5–7; avoid heavy clay (root rot)
grow.propagation: Grafting named cultivars onto seedling or clonal rootstocks
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–4 years from a grafted tree
steps: Buy a grafted tree; for best pollination, plant one 'A' type (e.g. 'Hass') and one 'B' type (e.g. 'Fuerte' or 'Bacon') near each other.
Plant on a raised mound in full sun with superb drainage; mulch thickly with wood chips but keep mulch off the trunk.
Water deeply but let the topsoil dry between waterings; protect young trees from frost and sunburn (whitewash the trunk).
Prune lightly to control height; avocados drop many fruitlets naturally.
Pick mature fruit (test one) and ripen indoors for 3–10 days; fruit can be 'stored' on the tree for months.

lore: The Nahuatl word āhuacatl also meant 'testicle', likely for the fruit's shape. The 'Hass' avocado, now about 80% of world trade, traces to a single seedling tree in the garden of postman Rudolph Hass in La Habra Heights, California, patented in 1935.
funFact: Every 'Hass' avocado in the world is a clone of one tree, which died in 2002.

summary: A fast-growing, short-lived, soft-stemmed tree that can fruit within a year of sowing. Native to Mesoamerica, it is now grown across the tropics, and its milky latex is the source of papain, an enzyme used to tenderise meat.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico and Central America; cultivated throughout the tropics
abilities: Grows from seed to fruiting tree 2–3 m tall in 6–12 months
Plants can be male, female or hermaphrodite, and some switch sex with temperature
Latex rich in papain digests proteins and protects the plant from insects
A genetically engineered virus-resistant papaya saved Hawaii's papaya industry from ringspot virus in the 1990s
edibleParts: green fruit (cooked or shredded in som tam salad)
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is safe. Unripe fruit and latex are high in papain and can irritate skin and the mouth; latex is traditionally avoided in pregnancy because it may stimulate uterine contractions.

uses.use: Leaf juice taken during dengue fever, with small trials suggesting raised platelet counts
Ripe fruit for digestion and constipation; seeds against intestinal worms
Green papaya poultice and latex on wounds and burns

medicinal.cautions: Unripe fruit and latex avoided in pregnancy. Latex allergy cross-reactivity. Seeds in large amounts may be harmful.

fruit.description: Oblong to pear-shaped berry 10–45 cm, green ripening yellow-orange; soft, sweet, musky orange-to-red flesh around a hollow cavity lined with seeds.

seed.description: Round, wrinkled, black seeds about 5 mm across, each wrapped in a clear, gelatinous sac (sarcotesta); hundreds per fruit, peppery-tasting
seed.germination: Wash off the jelly sac, sow 1 cm deep in warm (25–32 °C) free-draining mix; sprouts in 1–3 weeks

grow.water: Moderate; regular, never waterlogged
grow.soil: Light, very well-drained, rich in organic matter, pH 6–7
grow.propagation: Seed (choose seed from hermaphrodite fruit, e.g. 'Solo' types)
grow.timeToHarvest: 6–11 months from sowing
steps: Sow several seeds per pot of a hermaphrodite variety like 'Solo' or 'Red Lady' so most plants will fruit.
Plant out 2–3 m apart into a warm, sunny, wind-sheltered spot on a raised mound, as roots rot easily.
Feed every month with balanced fertiliser and mulch; water deeply in dry weather.
Once flowers appear, remove male-only plants (long-stalked flower clusters), keeping one per 10–20 if you grow dioecious types.
Harvest when the skin starts to turn yellow and ripen at room temperature; replace trees after 3–4 years as they grow tall.

lore: Christopher Columbus is said to have called the papaya 'the fruit of the angels'. Spanish and Portuguese sailors spread it across the tropics in the 16th century, reaching the Philippines and India by the 1600s.
funFact: Chymopapain from papaya latex was once injected to dissolve slipped spinal discs, and papain is still sold as meat tenderiser.

summary: A towering Southeast Asian rainforest tree famous for spiky fruit with a smell banned on many trains and hotels, yet a custardy flesh revered as the 'king of fruits'. Its flowers open at dusk and are pollinated mainly by fruit bats.
nativeRange: Borneo, Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula; cultivated across Southeast Asia
abilities: Pollinated chiefly by nectar bats such as the cave nectar bat (Eonycteris spelaea)
Odour comes from dozens of volatile sulphur compounds and esters
Trees grow 25–50 m tall in the wild
Ripe fruit falls from the tree on its own — it is gathered from the ground
edibilityNote: Flesh and cooked seeds are eaten; raw seeds are not. Traditional belief, with some lab support, warns against combining durian with alcohol, as it may inhibit alcohol breakdown.

uses.use: Leaf and root decoctions given for fever and jaundice
Considered a 'heating' food, balanced by eating 'cooling' mangosteen

medicinal.cautions: Avoid with alcohol. High in sugar and calories.

fruit.season: Varies; main seasons June–August in Malaysia and Thailand
fruit.description: Oval to round fruit 15–30 cm and 1–3 kg, covered in hard pyramidal thorns, green to brown; splits into five sections with creamy yellow, custard-like arils that smell strongly of onion, cheese and fruit.

seed.description: Glossy, chestnut-brown, oval to kidney-shaped seeds 2–4 cm long, enclosed in the soft aril; 1–7 per section
seed.dispersal: Orangutans, elephants, tigers, bears and other large mammals
seed.germination: Recalcitrant — sow fresh within days, 1–2 cm deep, at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 1–3 weeks

grow.sun: Full sun when mature; shade for young plants
grow.water: High, with a short dry spell to trigger flowering
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained, rich loam, pH 5–6.5
grow.propagation: Grafting (cleft, approach) of named cultivars such as 'Musang King' or 'Monthong' onto seedling rootstock
grow.timeToHarvest: 4–6 years from graft; 8–15 years from seed
steps: Buy a grafted tree of a named clone; plant 8–10 m apart in deep soil with excellent drainage, as durian is prone to Phytophthora root rot.
Shade young trees for the first 1–2 years and keep the soil mulched and moist.
Feed regularly with compost and balanced fertiliser; plant other durian clones nearby for better cross-pollination.
Prune to a single leader with well-spaced lateral branches for fruit to hang on.
Collect fruit as it falls (or tie fruit to branches with nets), and eat within 2–3 days.

lore: Naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating durian was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East'. Singapore's Esplanade concert hall is nicknamed 'the Durian' for its spiky roof.
funFact: Durian is banned on Singapore's metro trains, where signs show it alongside smoking and flammable goods.

summary: Jackfruit bears the largest tree-borne fruit in the world, up to 50 kg and nearly a metre long, hanging straight from the trunk. It is the national fruit of Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, eaten ripe as a sweet fruit and green as a meaty vegetable.
nativeRange: Western Ghats of south-west India; cultivated throughout South and Southeast Asia, East Africa, Brazil and the Caribbean
abilities: Produces the largest fruit borne by any tree, up to about 50 kg
Cauliflorous: fruit grows on the trunk and main limbs, which can bear the weight
A single tree can yield 100–200 fruit a year
Heartwood yields a saffron-yellow dye used for Buddhist monks' robes
edibleParts: unripe fruit (cooked as a vegetable or meat substitute)
edibilityNote: All main parts are eaten. Sticky white latex in the rind and core is not poisonous but is very gluey; oil hands and knives before cutting. Raw seeds contain trypsin inhibitors and should be cooked.

uses.use: Ripe fruit as a cooling, nourishing tonic; leaf ash applied to ulcers
Leaf decoction used for diabetes, with small studies on blood-sugar effects

medicinal.cautions: Latex allergy cross-reactions; birch-pollen allergy cross-reactivity reported.

fruit.description: Huge oblong fruit 30–90 cm, green to yellow-brown, covered in blunt hexagonal spines; inside, dozens of golden, sweet, fibrous bulbs among stringy 'rags', smelling of banana and pineapple.

seed.description: Smooth, light-brown, oval to kidney-shaped seeds 2–4 cm long, each inside a fleshy bulb and covered by a thin white membrane; up to several hundred per fruit
seed.germination: Recalcitrant: sow fresh within a month, 2 cm deep at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 2–6 weeks. Taproot dislikes transplanting

grow.water: Moderate–high; tolerates a dry season but not waterlogging
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained loam or sandy soil, pH 5–7.5
grow.propagation: Seed (variable), or grafted/budded named varieties
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–4 years from graft; 4–8 years from seed
steps: Plant a grafted tree or sow fresh seed directly where it will grow (8–10 m from buildings).
Water well for the first two years and mulch heavily; feed young trees with compost every few months.
Prune early to keep the tree low (4–6 m) and open, so fruit forms within reach on the trunk.
Thin to one or two fruit per cluster; tie heavy fruit with cloth slings if branches are weak.
Harvest when the spines flatten slightly, the fruit sounds hollow when tapped and it gives off a sweet smell; for vegetable use, pick young and green.

lore: Pliny the Elder, drawing on reports from Alexander's campaigns, described a huge Indian fruit eaten by sages that some identify as jackfruit (others as the banana), and it figures in the ancient Tamil 'mukkani' (three fruits) of mango, banana and jackfruit. Its wood is prized for temple furniture and veena lutes in South India.
funFact: The heaviest jackfruit on record, verified by Guinness World Records, weighed 42.72 kg and was grown in Hawaii in 2003.

summary: A Pacific staple domesticated from wild breadnut in New Guinea and carried by Polynesian voyagers across the ocean. Roasted, its starchy fruit tastes like fresh bread or potato, and one tree can feed a family for decades.
nativeRange: Domesticated from Artocarpus camansi in New Guinea and the Bismarck Archipelago; spread by humans across Oceania; now pantropical
abilities: Seedless Polynesian varieties survive only by human propagation from root cuttings
A mature tree can produce 150–200 fruit a season
Fruit can be fermented in pits and kept for months or years as emergency food
Latex used as caulking for canoes and as birdlime
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten cooked at the mature-starchy stage, or soft and sweet when fully ripe. Sticky latex is irritating.

uses.use: Latex applied to skin injuries, and diluted for diarrhoea
Yellowing leaf tea for high blood pressure

medicinal.cautions: Latex can irritate skin and eyes.

fruit.season: Main and secondary seasons; often almost year-round in the tropics
fruit.description: Round to oval fruit 10–30 cm and 1–5 kg, bright green with a patterned skin of hexagonal facets, turning yellow-brown; cream-white starchy flesh.

seed.description: Seedless in most Polynesian cultivars; seeded types hold brown, rounded to angular seeds about 1.5–2.5 cm, with a thin papery coat
seed.dispersal: Humans (root cuttings); bats for seeded forms
seed.germination: Seeds are recalcitrant and short-lived; most cultivars are propagated from root suckers

grow.water: High; 1,500–3,000 mm rain
grow.soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained; tolerates coral sands and slight salinity in some varieties
grow.propagation: Root cuttings or suckers; air layering; tissue culture
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–6 years
steps: Dig a 2–3 cm-thick section of surface root, cut into 20–25 cm lengths and lay in moist sand in shade until shoots appear (2–5 months).
Plant out in a warm, sheltered, sunny spot 10–12 m from other trees when shoots are 50–60 cm.
Mulch thickly and water during dry spells; protect from strong wind.
Prune to keep the tree under about 6 m for easy picking.
Harvest when small drops of latex appear on the skin; cook within 1–2 days, as fruit spoils quickly.

lore: William Bligh's 1789 voyage on HMS Bounty to carry breadfruit from Tahiti to the Caribbean as cheap food for enslaved people ended in the famous mutiny; he succeeded on a second voyage in 1793. In Hawaiian tradition the god Kū became a breadfruit tree to save his starving family.
funFact: Breadfruit was carried by Polynesian navigators across more than 10,000 km of open ocean as living root cuttings.

summary: The 'tree of life' of tropical coasts, providing food, drink, oil, fibre, thatch and timber. Its buoyant, waterproof fruit can drift on ocean currents for months and still germinate on a distant beach.
nativeRange: Indo-Pacific; domesticated separately in the Pacific and South Asia; now pantropical on coasts
abilities: Fruit floats and survives seawater for over 100 days, colonising islands
Tolerates salt spray, sandy soil and brackish groundwater
Coconut water inside a young nut is sterile and has been used as an emergency IV fluid
A single palm can yield 50–100 nuts a year for 60–80 years
edibleParts: meat (fresh, dried as copra, pressed for milk and oil)
edibilityNote: All these parts are widely eaten. Coconut oil is very high in saturated fat. Falling nuts are a real hazard — don't stand under laden palms.

uses.use: Coconut water for heat, thirst and urinary complaints; oil for hair and skin
Young coconut water as a rehydrating drink for illness
Coconut water used as emergency intravenous fluid in the Pacific

medicinal.cautions: Rare tree-nut-type allergy. Coconut oil raises LDL cholesterol.

fruit.description: Large ovoid drupe 20–30 cm with a smooth green, yellow or orange skin, a thick fibrous husk (coir) and a hard brown shell with three 'eyes', holding white meat and clear water.

seed.description: The 'coconut' of the market is the seed inside its hard, hairy brown endocarp, round, 10–15 cm across, with three dark germination pores at one end; inside is a layer of white endosperm (meat) and liquid endosperm (water)
seed.germination: Lay a whole mature husked nut on its side, half-buried in moist sandy soil in warm shade; shoots in 3–6 months

grow.water: Moderate–high; tolerates brackish water
grow.soil: Sandy, well-drained; tolerates salinity, pH 5–8
grow.propagation: Whole mature nuts (seed)
grow.timeToHarvest: Dwarf varieties 3–4 years; tall varieties 6–10 years
steps: Choose a fully mature nut that sloshes when shaken; soak for 2–3 days, then half-bury it on its side in sandy soil.
When the shoot is 30–60 cm and roots emerge, transplant into a large hole in full sun, keeping the nut at soil level.
Water regularly for the first two years and mulch with old husks, which hold moisture.
Feed with potassium-rich fertiliser; remove dead fronds and old nuts safely.
Harvest green nuts at 6–7 months for water, or let them ripen and fall at about 12 months for mature meat.

lore: In Hindu ritual a coconut is broken before the deity as an offering, symbolising the breaking of the ego, and Tamil and Malayali tradition calls it the 'kalpavriksha', the wish-fulfilling tree. Marco Polo described the 'nux indica' in the 13th century.
funFact: The word 'coco' comes from Portuguese for a grinning face or goblin, after the three dark eyes on the shell.

summary: A spiny terrestrial bromeliad from South America whose 'fruit' is a fusion of 100–200 individual berries around a central stalk. Its CAM photosynthesis lets it open its pores only at night, making it extraordinarily water-efficient.
nativeRange: Southern Brazil and Paraguay (Paraná–Paraguay basin); domesticated by Indigenous South Americans and spread pantropically
abilities: CAM photosynthesis: takes in CO₂ at night to save water
Fruit forms from up to 200 fused flowers, each 'eye' a separate berry
Hummingbirds pollinate wild plants; cultivated plants are self-incompatible, so fruit is seedless
Leaves yield piña fibre, woven into fine sheer cloth in the Philippines
edibleParts: fruit (fresh, cooked, juiced, fermented as tepache)
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is eaten. Bromelain makes the mouth tingle or sore when large amounts are eaten raw. Very unripe fruit is irritating and purgative.

uses.use: Fruit applied to wounds and taken for digestive troubles
Bromelain-based enzyme (NexoBrid) approved in Europe and the US for removing burn eschar

medicinal.cautions: Bromelain may increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants; pineapple allergy and latex cross-reactivity occur.

fruit.season: Year-round in the tropics; can be forced
fruit.description: Oval fruit 15–30 cm, covered in hexagonal scales ('eyes'), green ripening to golden-orange, topped with a crown of spiny leaves; juicy yellow flesh around a fibrous core.

seed.description: Usually absent in cultivated fruit; when cross-pollinated, small hard seeds appear just under the skin — dark brown to black, 3–5 mm, angular-oval
seed.germination: Seed rarely used; crowns, slips and suckers root easily

grow.zones: USDA 10–12 (11–12 outdoors year-round; also grown in pots indoors)
grow.water: Low–moderate
grow.soil: Sandy, acidic (pH 4.5–6.5), very well-drained
grow.propagation: Crowns, slips (shoots below the fruit) or suckers
grow.timeToHarvest: 18–24 months from a crown; 12–18 months from suckers
steps: Twist the leafy crown off a ripe pineapple, strip the bottom 3 cm of leaves and let it dry for 2–3 days.
Plant it 5 cm deep in sandy, acidic mix in full sun; water lightly, also into the leaf cup.
Feed lightly every 2 months; keep frost-free and above 15 °C.
To force flowering on a mature plant (12+ months), enclose it in a bag with a ripe apple for a few days, as the ethylene triggers blooming.
Harvest when the fruit smells sweet at the base and the eyes flatten and turn golden; the plant then produces suckers for the next crop.

lore: Columbus encountered the pineapple on Guadeloupe in 1493, and it became an emblem of luxury in 17th–18th century Europe, where wealthy hosts rented pineapples as table centrepieces. The Dunmore Pineapple in Scotland is a 1761 garden folly shaped like the fruit.
funFact: Pineapple's bromelain digests proteins so well that fresh pineapple stops gelatin from setting.

summary: The garden strawberry is an 18th-century accident: a hybrid of a Chilean and a North American wild strawberry that crossed in a French garden around 1750. The red flesh is a swollen receptacle — the true fruits are the tiny 'seeds' on the outside.
nativeRange: Hybrid of cultivated origin (Brittany, France, c. 1750) from F. chiloensis (Chile) and F. virginiana (North America); cultivated worldwide
abilities: Octoploid: carries eight sets of chromosomes
Spreads by runners (stolons) that root to form new clone plants
Each 'seed' on the surface is a separate achene, a true fruit
Day-neutral varieties fruit continuously regardless of day length
edibilityNote: Fruit and leaves are safe. Strawberries are a common trigger of allergy-like reactions in children.

uses.use: Leaf tea (mainly from wild strawberry) as a mild astringent for diarrhoea
Fruit to cool fevers and cleanse the teeth

medicinal.cautions: Can trigger hives and oral allergy in sensitive people.

fruit.season: Late spring to early summer; everbearers into autumn
fruit.description: Heart- to cone-shaped red fruit 2–5 cm, juicy and sweet, the swollen receptacle dotted with 200 or so tiny achenes.

seed.description: Tiny yellow to reddish-brown achenes, about 1 mm, egg-shaped, set in shallow pits on the outside of the berry
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 2–4 weeks, surface-sow (needs light) at 18–22 °C; 1–6 weeks. Seedlings differ from the parent except for seed-bred F1 varieties

grow.water: Moderate; keep evenly moist, especially as fruit swells
grow.soil: Rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5); raised beds ideal
grow.propagation: Rooted runners; certified virus-free plants; some varieties by seed
grow.timeToHarvest: 60–90 days from spring planting (everbearers) or the following spring (June-bearers)
steps: Buy certified disease-free plants and set them 30–45 cm apart in late summer or early spring, with the crown exactly at soil level.
Mulch with straw (hence the name) to keep fruit clean and the soil moist.
Remove flowers in the first spring on June-bearers to build strong plants; water at soil level to avoid grey mould.
Net against birds; pick fully red berries in the morning, with the cap on.
After harvest, trim old leaves, root a few runners into pots for new plants, and replace beds every 3–4 years.

lore: French spy and engineer Amédée-François Frézier brought Chilean strawberry plants to France in 1714; crossed with North American plants in Brittany, they produced the modern berry, named 'ananassa' for its supposed pineapple scent. Wimbledon has served strawberries and cream since 1877.
funFact: Botanically, a strawberry is not a berry — but a banana is.

summary: A deciduous shrub of eastern North American bogs and woods, domesticated only in the early 20th century. It needs strongly acidic soil and is pollinated best by bumblebees, which 'buzz' its bell-shaped flowers to shake out pollen.
nativeRange: Eastern North America from Nova Scotia to Florida and west to Texas; cultivated widely in temperate regions
abilities: Partners with ericoid mycorrhizal fungi that unlock nitrogen in acidic, nutrient-poor soil
Bell-shaped flowers release pollen best by sonication (buzz pollination)
Brilliant red autumn foliage
Blue colour comes from anthocyanins under a waxy bloom that scatters light
edibilityNote: Fruit is safe and widely eaten.

uses.use: Berries dried as winter food; root and leaf tea used in childbirth and as a blood purifier
Blueberry anthocyanins studied for memory and vascular health, with some positive small trials

medicinal.cautions: Leaf extracts may lower blood sugar.

fruit.description: Round berries 1–2 cm, dark blue with a pale waxy bloom and a five-pointed crown at the tip; sweet-tart, pale-green flesh.

seed.description: Tiny, soft, flattened brown seeds about 1 mm, 20–100 per berry, barely noticeable when eaten
seed.germination: Surface-sow on moist sphagnum or peat at 20 °C (light helps); 1–2 months. Rarely used outside breeding

grow.water: Moderate–high; shallow roots need constant moisture
grow.soil: Strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), loose, peaty, well-drained; add sulphur or plant in ericaceous compost
grow.propagation: Softwood or hardwood cuttings of named cultivars
grow.timeToHarvest: 2–3 years from planting; full crops at 5–6 years
steps: Test soil pH; if above 5.5, lower it with elemental sulphur months ahead or plant in a raised bed or large pot of ericaceous compost.
Plant two or more varieties (e.g. 'Bluecrop', 'Duke', 'Elliott') 1.5 m apart for better cross-pollination and bigger berries.
Mulch 10 cm deep with pine needles or bark and water with rainwater where tap water is hard.
Remove flowers in the first year; from year four, prune in late winter by cutting a few of the oldest canes to the ground.
Net against birds and pick berries a few days after they turn fully blue, when they fall off easily.

lore: Botanist Frederick Coville and New Jersey farmer Elizabeth White domesticated the highbush blueberry from wild bushes in the Pine Barrens between 1908 and 1916. Many Algonquian peoples dried the berries and mixed them into pemmican.
funFact: Elizabeth White paid local pickers to find the best wild bushes — one, found by Rube Leek, became the parent of early cultivars like 'Rubel'.

summary: A tall, glossy-barked European and West Asian tree whose wild form, the gean or mazzard, gave rise to all sweet cherries. Its spring blossom is a key early nectar source for bees, and birds spread its stones widely — hence 'avium', of the birds.
nativeRange: Europe, Anatolia, the Caucasus and north-west Africa; cultivated in temperate regions worldwide
abilities: Extrafloral nectaries on the leaf stalks attract ants that defend the tree
Bark peels in horizontal shining bands with conspicuous lenticels
Most varieties are self-incompatible and need a compatible pollinator variety
Wood is a fine-grained, reddish cabinet timber
edibilityNote: Flesh is safe. Crushed stones, leaves and bark contain cyanogenic glycosides; swallowed whole stones pass harmlessly, but crushed kernels in quantity are dangerous. Leaves are toxic to livestock.

uses.use: Cherry-stalk tea as a diuretic
Cherry stalks for kidney stones and fluid retention

medicinal.cautions: Kernels, leaves and bark are cyanogenic.

fruit.description: Round to heart-shaped drupe 1.5–3 cm on a long stalk, glossy deep red to almost black, or yellow-red in 'Rainier' types; sweet, juicy flesh around a smooth stone.

seed.description: A smooth, round to slightly oval, cream to pale-tan stone 7–10 mm, with a faint ridge; it holds one almond-like kernel
seed.germination: Needs 90–120 days moist cold stratification at 1–5 °C (or sow outdoors in autumn); sprouts in spring

grow.water: Moderate; avoid heavy watering near harvest (causes splitting)
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained loam, pH 6–7.5; dislikes wet clay
grow.propagation: Budding or grafting onto rootstocks such as 'Colt' or 'Gisela 5' (dwarfing)
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years on dwarfing rootstock
steps: Choose a self-fertile variety (e.g. 'Stella', 'Lapins') or plant two compatible varieties; use a dwarfing rootstock for easy netting.
Plant bare-root in winter in a sunny spot with good air drainage to avoid spring frost on blossom.
Water deeply in dry spells during fruit growth but ease off in the last week before harvest.
Prune only in summer, after fruiting, to reduce the risk of silver leaf and bacterial canker.
Net the tree as fruit colours, and pick cherries with stalks attached when fully coloured and sweet.

lore: Pliny says the Roman general Lucullus brought cherries to Rome from Kerasous (Giresun) on the Black Sea in 74 BCE, though wild cherries grew in Europe long before. Cherry stones are common finds at Bronze Age sites across Europe.
funFact: The Greek town name Kerasous may have given us the very word 'cherry', via Latin cerasum.

summary: Despite its name ('Persian plum'), the peach was domesticated in China's Yangtze valley about 7,500 years ago and reached Europe via Persia. Nectarines are the same species, differing by a single gene for smooth skin.
nativeRange: Northwest and central China; cultivated worldwide in temperate and subtropical climates
abilities: Self-fertile, unlike many relatives: a single tree sets fruit
Nectarines arise from a recessive mutation that removes the fuzz
Fruits on one-year-old wood, so it needs hard annual pruning
Kernels contain amygdalin, which yields cyanide
edibleParts: flowers (in salads and tea, small amounts)
edibilityNote: Flesh is safe. The kernel inside the stone, and the leaves and bark, contain cyanogenic glycosides and should not be eaten in quantity.

uses.use: Peach kernel (táo rén) used to 'invigorate blood' and relieve constipation, in prescribed doses
Leaf tea as a sedative and for coughs

medicinal.cautions: Kernels, leaves and bark are cyanogenic; peach-skin lipid-transfer protein is a common cause of serious fruit allergy in the Mediterranean.

fruit.description: Round drupe 5–9 cm with a groove along one side; velvety (or smooth in nectarines) yellow skin blushed red; juicy white or yellow flesh around a deeply pitted stone, 'clingstone' or 'freestone'.

seed.description: Hard, deeply furrowed and pitted, oval stone 2–3.5 cm, reddish-brown, with a pointed tip; holds a single almond-shaped, brown-skinned kernel
seed.germination: Remove kernel or crack the stone, cold-stratify 60–90 days at 2–5 °C, sow in spring; seedlings often give decent fruit

grow.water: Moderate; regular in dry spells while fruit swells
grow.soil: Sandy loam, well-drained, pH 6–7
grow.propagation: Budding onto peach seedling or 'St Julien A' rootstock; seed
grow.timeToHarvest: 2–4 years
steps: Choose a variety matched to your chill hours (e.g. 'Redhaven' for cold areas, 'Florida Prince' for low-chill areas), with resistance to peach leaf curl if possible.
Plant in the sunniest, warmest spot, ideally a fan trained against a south-facing wall in cool climates.
Prune to an open vase each year in late winter or just after bud-break, removing a third of old wood, as fruit grows only on last year's shoots.
Thin fruitlets to 15–20 cm apart when marble-sized for bigger, sweeter peaches.
In wet climates, cover with a rain shelter from late winter to spring to prevent leaf curl; pick when the fruit gives slightly near the stalk.

lore: In Chinese myth the Queen Mother of the West grows peaches of immortality that ripen once every 3,000 years, and the Monkey King steals them in Journey to the West. The 'Peach Blossom Spring' of the poet Tao Yuanming (421 CE) is China's archetypal hidden paradise.
funFact: Peach stones about 2.6 million years old have been found fossilised in Kunming, China, showing wild peaches existed long before humans.

summary: Named 'Armenian plum' by the Romans, the apricot actually originated in Central Asia and northern China. It is one of the first trees to bloom in spring, and in Hunza and Ladakh dried apricots and their kernel oil have long been winter staples.
nativeRange: Central Asia (Tian Shan, Dzungaria) and northern China; cultivated in Mediterranean and continental climates worldwide
abilities: Flowers very early, before the leaves, so blossom is often lost to late frost
Most cultivars are self-fertile
Tolerates hot dry summers and very cold continental winters in Central Asian types
Kernels contain amygdalin, which releases cyanide
edibleParts: sweet kernels of selected varieties (in moderation)
edibilityNote: Flesh is safe. Bitter apricot kernels are rich in amygdalin and have caused cyanide poisoning — a few bitter kernels can be dangerous to a child. Do not eat bitter kernels raw.

uses.use: Bitter apricot kernel (kǔ xìng rén) in small, prescribed doses for cough and wheezing
Dried apricots as a mild laxative and nutritive

medicinal.cautions: Bitter kernels are cyanogenic and poisonous; 'laetrile' from kernels is not an effective cancer treatment and has caused poisonings.

fruit.description: Round drupe 3–5 cm with a shallow groove, velvety yellow-orange skin often blushed red; sweet, slightly tart, firm orange flesh around a smooth flattened stone.

seed.description: Smooth, flattened oval stone 2–3 cm, light brown with a ridged edge; inside is a single almond-like kernel with a brown skin, sweet or bitter depending on variety
seed.germination: Cold-stratify the stone 60–90 days at 2–5 °C, sow in spring 3 cm deep; seedlings are variable but often fruit acceptably

grow.water: Low–moderate
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral (pH 6.5–8)
grow.propagation: Budding onto apricot, peach or plum rootstock; seed
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–4 years
steps: Choose a late-flowering variety if your area has spring frosts, and plant in a sunny but not frost-pocketed site.
Plant bare-root in winter; fan-train against a warm wall in cool climates.
Water deeply in dry spells during fruit growth; avoid wet soil around the trunk.
Prune in summer (after harvest) to reduce the risk of silver leaf and canker; thin fruit to 8–10 cm apart.
Pick when fully coloured and slightly soft; halve and sun-dry or dehydrate for keeping.

lore: Apricots reached Greece and Rome via Armenia, hence 'armeniaca', and Arab gardeners spread them through Spain. The Hunza people of Pakistan's Karakoram are famed for their apricot orchards, drying the fruit on rooftops each summer.
funFact: The word 'apricot' comes from Latin praecoquum, 'early-ripening', via Arabic al-barqūq and Spanish albaricoque.

summary: The tree that built the Silk Road: its leaves are the only food of the domestic silkworm, and China guarded sericulture as a state secret for millennia. Its catkins also fling pollen at over half the speed of sound, one of the fastest movements in the plant kingdom.
nativeRange: Northern and central China; cultivated and naturalised across Asia, Europe and the Americas
abilities: Stamens spring open like catapults in under 25 microseconds, flinging pollen at more than half the speed of sound
Leaves are the sole natural food of the silkworm Bombyx mori
Fruit colour varies from white to pink to near-black despite the name 'white'
Tolerates drought, pollution and poor soil; often invasive
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is safe; unripe fruit and the milky sap can cause stomach upset and mild hallucinogenic effects have been claimed for unripe fruit.

uses.use: Leaf (sāng yè) for colds and sore eyes, root bark (sāng bái pí) for cough, fruit (sāng shèn) as a blood tonic
Leaf extract containing 1-deoxynojirimycin studied for lowering post-meal blood sugar

medicinal.cautions: Leaf extract may lower blood sugar; caution with diabetes medication. Pollen is allergenic.

fruit.description: Blackberry-like cluster 1–2.5 cm long, white, pink, purple or black; very sweet and mild, staining if dark.

seed.description: Minute, pale-brown, lens-shaped seeds about 2 mm, one inside each tiny drupelet
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 4–8 weeks, then surface-sow lightly covered at 20–25 °C; 1–3 weeks

grow.water: Low–moderate
grow.soil: Any well-drained soil, pH 5.5–7.5
grow.propagation: Hardwood cuttings in winter, softwood cuttings in summer, grafting; seed
grow.timeToHarvest: 2–3 years from cuttings
steps: Take 20–30 cm hardwood cuttings from a good fruiting tree in winter and root them in moist soil, or buy a named variety (fruitless male clones are sold for shade — avoid those if you want fruit).
Plant away from paths and parking, as dark fruit stains everything.
Water young trees in dry spells; established trees need little care.
Prune in winter to shape; for silkworm leaf production, pollard annually.
Shake ripe fruit onto a sheet spread beneath the tree; eat or freeze promptly.

lore: Chinese legend credits Empress Leizu with discovering silk around 2700 BCE when a cocoon fell into her tea beneath a mulberry tree. In 552 CE two monks smuggled silkworm eggs to Constantinople in hollow canes, breaking China's monopoly.
funFact: The white mulberry's pollen-launching stamens move at roughly half the speed of sound — among the fastest motions known in plants.

summary: A relative of ebony, cultivated in China for over 2,000 years for its glowing orange fruit that hangs on bare branches into winter. Astringent varieties are inedibly puckering until soft-ripe; non-astringent types like 'Fuyu' can be eaten crisp like an apple.
nativeRange: China; long cultivated in Japan and Korea, now grown in warm-temperate regions worldwide
abilities: Soluble tannins in unripe astringent fruit bind proteins in the mouth, causing a dry pucker
Fruit can set without pollination (parthenocarpy), giving seedless fruit
Fruit hangs on leafless branches well into winter
Unripe juice (kakishibu) is fermented into a waterproofing dye for paper and cloth
edibleParts: fruit (fresh, or dried as hoshigaki / shìbǐng)
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is safe. Eating lots of unripe astringent persimmons, especially on an empty stomach, can form hard stomach masses (diospyrobezoars) that may need surgery.

uses.use: Dried calyx (shì dì) used for hiccups; dried fruit for cough
Persimmon-leaf tea, rich in vitamin C, as a tonic

medicinal.cautions: Bezoar risk from large amounts of unripe fruit, especially after stomach surgery.

fruit.description: Round to acorn-shaped berry 5–9 cm, glossy orange to red-orange, with a persistent four-lobed green calyx; flesh orange, jelly-soft when ripe or crisp in non-astringent types.

seed.description: Flattened, oblong, dark-brown seeds 1.5–2 cm long, smooth and hard; 0–8 per fruit, often none
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 60–90 days, sow 2 cm deep at 20–25 °C; slow and taprooted, 3–8 weeks

grow.water: Moderate; even moisture reduces fruit drop
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained loam, pH 6–7.5; tolerates clay if drained
grow.propagation: Grafting onto D. kaki, D. lotus or D. virginiana seedling rootstocks
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years from a grafted tree
steps: Choose a variety: non-astringent ('Fuyu', 'Jiro') to eat crisp, or astringent ('Hachiya') to eat soft or dry.
Plant a grafted tree in full sun, sheltered from strong wind, which damages brittle branches.
Water regularly in the first years and during fruit swell; feed lightly, as excess nitrogen causes fruit drop.
Prune lightly in winter to thin crowded branches; thin heavy crops to prevent limb breakage.
Cut fruit with a short stalk; ripen astringent types until jelly-soft, or peel and hang them to dry as hoshigaki.

lore: Persimmon trees that survived the atomic bombing of Nagasaki have been propagated as 'Kaki Tree Project' saplings planted in schools worldwide. In Korea, dried persimmon (gotgam) is offered at ancestral rites during Chuseok.
funFact: Diospyros means 'fruit of the gods' (or 'grain of Zeus') in Greek.

summary: A handsome evergreen of southern China whose fruit was so treasured that Tang dynasty relay riders galloped them over 1,000 km to the court. Under a rough red skin lies translucent, perfumed white flesh.
nativeRange: Guangdong, Fujian and Hainan, southern China, and northern Vietnam; cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions
abilities: Needs a cool, dry winter period to flower reliably
Fruit does not ripen further after picking
Flowers are a major honey source in South China
Unripe fruit contains hypoglycin A and MCPG, which lower blood sugar
