edibilityNote: Ripe flesh is safe. Unripe lychees contain hypoglycin A and MCPG; eating many on an empty stomach has caused severe hypoglycaemia and deaths among undernourished children in Muzaffarpur, India, and in Vietnam. Seeds are not eaten.

uses.use: Seed (lì zhī hé) to relieve hernia and testicular pain; fruit considered warming

medicinal.cautions: Do not let malnourished children eat many lychees on an empty stomach; seeds are toxic.

fruit.season: Late spring to summer (May–July in the Northern Hemisphere)
fruit.description: Round to heart-shaped fruit 3–4 cm, rough pinkish-red bumpy skin that peels easily; juicy, translucent white aril with a rose-like scent.

seed.description: Glossy, smooth, deep mahogany-brown seed, oval, 1.5–2.5 cm; 'chicken-tongue' varieties have shrivelled seeds only a few mm long
seed.germination: Recalcitrant: sow within a few days, 1–2 cm deep at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 1–3 weeks; seedlings take 8–12 years to fruit

grow.water: Moderate–high in summer; drier in late autumn–winter to induce flowering
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5–6.5), rich in organic matter
grow.propagation: Air layering (marcotting) — the traditional method; grafting
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years from an air-layer
steps: Buy an air-layered tree of a reliable variety (e.g. 'Mauritius', 'Brewster', 'Kwai Mai Pink').
Plant in a sunny, wind-sheltered spot, and mix in soil from under an existing lychee if possible, as it carries helpful mycorrhizal fungi.
Water regularly in the growing season, then withhold water and fertiliser for 2–3 months in autumn/winter so the tree flowers.
Net trees against birds and bats as fruit colours.
Cut whole clusters with a bit of stem when fruit is fully red and sweet; refrigerate, as skins brown within days.

lore: The Tang emperor Xuanzong had fresh lychees rushed by relay horse to his consort Yang Guifei, a luxury the poet Du Mu lamented. Cai Xiang's 'Lizhi Pu' (1059 CE) is often called the world's first monograph on a fruit tree.
funFact: Cai Xiang's 11th-century 'Treatise on Lychees' lists 32 named varieties.

summary: A tough, small tropical American tree with peeling coppery bark and intensely fragrant fruit, often far richer in vitamin C than an orange. It thrives so well that it has become an invasive weed on many tropical islands.
nativeRange: Tropical America from Mexico to northern South America; naturalised throughout the tropics
abilities: Fruits within 2–4 years from seed and can crop twice a year
Tolerates drought, poor soils and periodic flooding
Spreads rapidly via bird- and pig-dispersed seed, invading Pacific islands such as the Galápagos
Peeling, mottled coppery bark sheds in thin flakes
edibilityNote: Fruit, skin and seeds are eaten. Seeds are hard; eating many can cause constipation.

uses.use: Guava-leaf tea for diarrhoea and stomach ache
Leaf chewed or used as mouthwash for toothache and mouth ulcers
Guava-leaf polyphenol tea (approved FOSHU) for moderating post-meal blood sugar

medicinal.cautions: Leaf extracts may lower blood sugar.

fruit.season: Varies; often two crops a year (summer and winter)
fruit.description: Round to pear-shaped berry 4–12 cm, green to yellow skin; white, pink or red flesh, musky-sweet, with a central pulp full of seeds.

seed.description: Many small, hard, kidney-shaped to angular seeds, cream to pale-yellow, 3–5 mm, embedded in the central pulp
seed.germination: Soak 2 weeks or boil briefly to soften the coat, sow at 25–30 °C; 2–8 weeks

grow.water: Moderate; tolerates drought but fruits better with regular water
grow.soil: Adaptable — sand, clay, limestone; pH 5–7
grow.propagation: Air layering, cuttings, grafting; seed
grow.timeToHarvest: 2–4 years from seed, 1–2 years from layers
steps: Plant an air-layered or grafted plant of a good variety ('Allahabad Safeda', 'Ruby Supreme') in full sun.
Water regularly while establishing; mulch and feed every few months with balanced fertiliser.
Prune after each crop to keep the tree 2–3 m tall and open; fruit forms on new growth.
Bag young fruit with paper or mesh in areas with fruit flies.
Pick when the skin turns from dark to light green or yellow and the fruit smells strongly; ripen at room temperature.

lore: Spanish chronicler Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo described guavas in the Caribbean in 1526, and the Portuguese carried them to India, where Allahabad guavas became famous. Guava paste eaten with cheese ('Romeo y Julieta') is a classic in Brazil and the Caribbean.
funFact: Guava fruit can hold about four times the vitamin C of an orange by weight — roughly 228 mg per 100 g.

summary: A vigorous tendril-climbing vine from South America with elaborate fringed flowers that Spanish missionaries read as symbols of Christ's Passion. Its wrinkled purple or yellow fruit holds fragrant, tangy pulp around crunchy black seeds.
nativeRange: Southern Brazil, Paraguay and northern Argentina; cultivated throughout the tropics and subtropics
abilities: Flowers last a single day and are pollinated mainly by carpenter bees (Xylocopa)
Climbs fast with coiling tendrils, covering a fence in a season
Yellow form (flavicarpa) is largely self-incompatible and needs cross-pollination
Leaves and unripe fruit contain cyanogenic glycosides
edibilityNote: Ripe pulp and seeds are safe. Leaves, stems and very unripe fruit contain cyanogenic glycosides and should not be eaten.

uses.use: Leaf tea ('maracujá') as a calming sedative
Leaves and flowers as a remedy for sleeplessness and nerves

medicinal.cautions: Leaves are cyanogenic; sedative leaf preparations may add to sedative drugs.

fruit.season: Summer to autumn; often two crops in the tropics
fruit.description: Round to egg-shaped berry 4–8 cm, smooth skin turning deep purple or yellow and wrinkling when ripe; hollow inside, filled with juicy golden pulp sacs around seeds.

seed.description: Flat, oval, black seeds 5–6 mm, with a finely pitted surface, each enclosed in a juicy yellow-orange aril
seed.germination: Clean off pulp, soak 1–2 days, sow 0.5 cm deep at 20–30 °C; 2–4 weeks

grow.water: Moderate–high; regular
grow.soil: Light, well-drained, rich in organic matter, pH 6–7.5
grow.propagation: Seed, cuttings, or grafting onto disease-resistant yellow rootstock
grow.timeToHarvest: 12–18 months from seed
steps: Sow seed or plant a grafted vine next to a sturdy trellis, fence or pergola at least 2 m tall.
Train the main stem up to the top wire, then let side shoots hang down — fruit forms on new growth.
Water deeply and feed every 1–2 months in the growing season with a balanced fertiliser; mulch roots.
Prune lightly after harvest to remove old, tangled growth; hand-pollinate yellow forms in the afternoon if carpenter bees are scarce.
Gather fruit as it falls or when it colours fully; let it wrinkle for a few days for the sweetest pulp.

lore: In the 17th century Jesuit missionaries saw the corona as the crown of thorns, the five anthers as Christ's wounds and the three styles as the nails, calling it 'flos passionis' — the root of the genus name Passiflora. Brazil is today the world's largest producer.
funFact: The name has nothing to do with romance — it refers to the Passion (suffering) of Christ.

summary: A vigorous woody climber of China's Yangtze valley forests, brought to New Zealand in 1904 by schoolteacher Isabel Fraser and rebranded 'kiwifruit' in 1959 for export. iNaturalist treats it as a variety of Actinidia chinensis.
nativeRange: Central and south-west China (Shaanxi, Sichuan, Hubei, Henan); cultivated in New Zealand, Italy, Chile and elsewhere
abilities: Dioecious: separate male and female vines; one male pollinates up to about eight females
Flowers produce no nectar, so bees visit only for pollen
Contains actinidin, a protease that tenderises meat and stops gelatin from setting
Twining stems can climb 9 m or more
edibilityNote: Fruit and fuzzy skin are edible. Kiwi allergy is relatively common and can be severe, especially in children; actinidin may make the mouth sore.

uses.use: Fruit to clear heat and quench thirst; root in folk remedies
Two kiwifruit a day shown in trials to ease chronic constipation; EU-authorised claim for normal bowel function (green kiwi)

medicinal.cautions: Common food allergen; cross-reacts with latex, birch pollen and other fruits.

fruit.description: Oval berry 5–8 cm with thin brown skin covered in stiff hairs; bright emerald-green flesh with a pale core ringed by tiny black seeds.

seed.description: Tiny, flattened, oval, black to dark-brown seeds about 1.5–2 mm, arranged in a ring around the white core; over 1,000 per fruit
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 4–8 weeks, surface-sow at 20–25 °C; 2–4 weeks. Half of seedlings will be male; fruiting takes 4–7 years

grow.sun: Full sun, with shelter from strong wind
grow.water: High; regular deep watering in summer
grow.soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–7)
grow.propagation: Grafting or cuttings of named female cultivars (e.g. 'Hayward') and male pollinisers
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years
steps: Plant at least one male vine (e.g. 'Tomuri') for every 6–8 female vines (e.g. 'Hayward'), 4–5 m apart.
Build a strong T-bar trellis or pergola about 1.8 m high before planting — mature vines are very heavy.
Train one trunk to the wire, then two permanent arms (cordons) along it; fruiting canes hang from these.
Prune hard in winter, cutting fruited canes back and tying in new canes; summer-prune to control vigour. Protect spring shoots from late frost.
Pick firm in autumn when seeds are black and sugars reach about 6.5 °Brix; ripen in a bag with an apple at room temperature.

lore: The botanist E. H. Wilson collected it in Hubei in 1900, and Isabel Fraser carried seeds home to Whanganui, New Zealand, from a mission school in Yichang in 1904. In 1959 New Zealand exporter Turners & Growers renamed it 'kiwifruit', after the national bird, partly to avoid US tariffs on 'melons' and 'berries'.
funFact: Almost all green kiwifruit sold worldwide is the single cultivar 'Hayward', bred by Hayward Wright in Auckland in the 1920s.

summary: A small, crooked tree whose hard, golden, perfumed fruit is almost inedible raw but turns rosy-pink and fragrant when slowly cooked. The quince was the 'golden apple' of much ancient Greek myth, and its jelly-like paste gave the world the word 'marmalade'.
nativeRange: The Caucasus, northern Iran, Turkmenistan and adjacent West Asia; cultivated across Europe, West and Central Asia and South America
abilities: Fruit flesh turns from white to deep pink-red when cooked long, as tannins convert to anthocyanin-like pigments
Self-fertile; large single flowers appear after the leaves, escaping most frosts
Used worldwide as a dwarfing rootstock for pears
Seed coat produces a thick mucilage when soaked
edibleParts: fruit (cooked into paste, jelly, stews; raw in mild varieties)
edibilityNote: Fruit is safe, mostly cooked. Seeds contain amygdalin and should not be crushed or eaten; whole soaked seeds are used only for their outer mucilage.

uses.use: Bihidana (quince-seed mucilage) for sore throats, coughs and dry skin
Quince syrup for nausea, vomiting and reflux; small trials report benefit in GERD

medicinal.cautions: Do not crush or eat seeds (cyanogenic).

fruit.description: Large pear- or apple-shaped pome 7–12 cm, covered in grey down when young, ripening to golden yellow and intensely fragrant; hard, astringent, gritty cream flesh.

seed.description: Many dark-brown, glossy, wedge-shaped seeds about 6–8 mm, packed in the five core chambers and coated in a gel that swells when wet
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 60–90 days, sow in spring; usually propagated vegetatively

grow.water: Moderate; tolerates damp soil better than apples
grow.soil: Deep, moist, well-drained loam, pH 6–7; becomes chlorotic on chalk
grow.propagation: Hardwood cuttings, layering, budding onto quince rootstock
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years
steps: Plant a named variety (e.g. 'Vranja', 'Meech's Prolific', 'Isfahan') in full sun in moist but well-drained soil.
Water during dry summers; a single tree is enough as quinces are self-fertile.
Prune lightly in winter just to thin crowded and crossing branches — fruit forms at the tips of shoots, so avoid hard tip pruning.
Watch for fireblight and leaf blight; remove infected shoots promptly.
Pick in mid-to-late autumn when fully yellow and fragrant, before hard frost; store separately as their scent taints other fruit.

lore: Plutarch records that Solon's laws had Athenian brides eat a quince before entering the bridal chamber, and many scholars think the golden apples of the Hesperides were quinces. Portuguese 'marmelada', quince paste, gave English its word marmalade.
funFact: A ripe quince left in a room will perfume it for weeks — medieval Europeans kept them in linen chests.

otherNames: Hassomin (Algonquian, origin of the genus name)
summary: The largest edible fruit native to the United States, a temperate member of the tropical custard-apple family. Its maroon flowers smell faintly of rotting meat to attract carrion flies and beetles, and its fruit tastes of banana, mango and custard.
nativeRange: Eastern United States and southern Ontario, from the Great Lakes to the Gulf Coast
abilities: Forms clonal thickets (patches) by root suckers
Leaves and bark contain acetogenins that deter most herbivores and insects
Pawpaws and their Asimina relatives are the only host plants for zebra swallowtail caterpillars, which store their toxins for defence
Flowers are pollinated by flies and beetles drawn to a fermenting, yeasty scent
edibilityNote: Ripe flesh is eaten fresh or frozen. Skin and seeds contain annonaceous acetogenins and should not be eaten; seeds are toxic if chewed. Some people get stomach upset or skin rashes from handling the fruit.

uses.tradition: Cherokee and other Indigenous American medicine
uses.use: Seeds and bark preparations used to treat lice and as an emetic
Twig extract acetogenins (asimicin) studied for pesticidal and anticancer activity in the lab

medicinal.cautions: Annonacin is a neurotoxin linked to atypical parkinsonism in heavy consumers of related Annona fruit; avoid seeds, skin and concentrated extracts.

fruit.description: Oblong, slightly kidney-shaped berry 5–16 cm, green ripening to yellowish with dark flecks, often in clusters; soft, custardy, pale-yellow to orange flesh.

seed.description: Large, flattened, bean-like seeds 2–3 cm long, glossy dark brown, in two rows of 10–14 inside the fruit
seed.dispersal: Raccoons, opossums, foxes, bears and formerly megafauna
seed.germination: Never let seeds dry; cold-stratify moist for 90–120 days, then sow 2–3 cm deep in deep pots at 25 °C. Shoots emerge slowly (6–10 weeks) after a long taproot forms

grow.sun: Shade when young (first 1–2 years); full sun for best fruiting
grow.water: Moderate–high; likes moist soil
grow.soil: Deep, fertile, moist but well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–7)
grow.propagation: Seed (after cold stratification), or grafting named cultivars ('Shenandoah', 'Susquehanna', 'Sunflower')
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–4 years from graft; 5–8 years from seed
steps: Plant at least two genetically different trees (two grafted cultivars or seedlings), as pawpaws are self-incompatible.
Use container-grown plants — the long taproot resents digging — and shade them with a tube or cloth for the first summer.
Keep soil moist and mulched; feed lightly with compost.
If fruit set is poor, hand-pollinate with a small brush, or hang rotting meat or fish nearby to attract flies (a traditional trick).
Pick when fruit gives gently like a ripe peach and smells fruity; eat within 2–3 days or freeze the pulp.

lore: In 1541 the de Soto expedition found Native Americans growing and eating what was probably pawpaw east of the Mississippi, and Lewis and Clark relied on pawpaws when food ran short in 1806. A popular but undocumented story makes chilled pawpaw George Washington's favourite dessert.
funFact: Pawpaw is the largest fruit native to North America, sometimes reaching 0.5 kg.

summary: A long-lived, drought-hardy legume tree from tropical Africa whose brown pods hold a sticky, sweet-sour pulp essential to South Indian, Thai, Mexican and Middle Eastern cooking. Its very name comes from the Arabic 'tamar hindi', Indian date.
nativeRange: Tropical Africa (Sudan and the Sahel to East Africa and Madagascar); naturalised and cultivated throughout the tropics, especially India
abilities: Pulp is among the most acidic fruit pulps known, rich in tartaric acid, yet also very sugary
Withstands long droughts, strong winds and cyclones
Leaflets fold together at night
Trees can live and fruit for over 200 years
edibleParts: pod pulp (fresh, dried, as paste or drinks)
edibilityNote: Pulp, leaves and flowers are eaten. Seeds must be roasted or boiled and peeled before eating.

uses.use: Ripe pulp as a mild laxative and digestive
Pulp drinks for fever and to treat sunstroke
Tamarind sherbet as a cooling remedy for bilious complaints

medicinal.cautions: Laxative in quantity; may increase absorption of aspirin and ibuprofen.

fruit.description: Curved, bean-like pod 5–15 cm with a brittle cinnamon-brown shell; inside, sticky brown sweet-sour pulp laced with fibres around 3–10 seeds.

seed.description: Hard, glossy, dark reddish-brown to chocolate seeds, flattened and irregularly squarish-rhomboid, about 1–1.5 cm
seed.germination: Nick or soak in hot water overnight, sow 2 cm deep at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 1–2 weeks

grow.zones: USDA 10–12 (mature trees tolerate brief light frost)
grow.water: Low once established
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained; tolerates poor, sandy and slightly saline soils, pH 5–8
grow.propagation: Seed, or grafting / air layering of sweet varieties
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years from graft; 7–10 years from seed
steps: Soak seeds overnight in warm water and sow in deep pots, or buy a grafted 'sweet tamarind' tree.
Plant out in full sun with plenty of space (it can reach 20 m and spread widely).
Water regularly for the first two years, then only during prolonged drought.
Prune young trees to shape a strong framework; little pruning is needed later.
Harvest pods when the shell is brittle and brown; shell them, remove strings and seeds, and press the pulp into blocks for storage.

lore: Tamarind reached India so long ago that it appears in Sanskrit texts as 'amlika', and Arab traders named it 'Indian date'. In Myanmar and India, folklore warns not to sleep beneath a tamarind tree, said to harbour spirits.
funFact: Tamarind is one of the listed ingredients that gives Worcestershire sauce its tangy depth.

summary: A thorny, zigzag-branched small tree cultivated in northern China for over 4,000 years. Its fruit, eaten crisp like an apple or dried into chewy 'red dates', is a cornerstone of Chinese cooking and medicine.
nativeRange: Northern China (probably the middle Yellow River valley); cultivated across East, Central and West Asia, the Mediterranean and North America
abilities: Survives extreme heat, cold to about −28 °C, drought and alkaline or saline soil
Leafs out late in spring, so it escapes frost damage to flowers
Paired spines, one straight and one hooked, guard each node in wild forms
Spreads by root suckers into thickets
edibilityNote: Fruit is safe and widely eaten. Seeds are used only medicinally.

uses.use: Dried fruit (dà zǎo) to tonify qi and blood and harmonise herbal formulas; seed (suān zǎo rén, from the sour jujube) for insomnia and anxiety
Unnab fruit decoction for coughs, sore throat and as a blood purifier

medicinal.cautions: Seed preparations are sedative and may add to sedative medicines.

fruit.description: Oval to round drupe 2–5 cm, glossy green ripening to mahogany-red; crisp, sweet, apple-like white flesh that wrinkles and turns date-like when dried, around a single stone.

seed.description: Hard, elongated, pointed-oval stone 1–2 cm, reddish-brown and roughly ridged, holding one or two small flat brown seeds
seed.germination: Crack or scarify the stone, cold-stratify 60–90 days, sow at 20–25 °C; erratic. Named varieties are grafted

grow.sun: Full sun; needs summer heat to fruit well
grow.water: Low once established
grow.soil: Any well-drained soil, including alkaline, saline or poor, pH 5.5–8.5
grow.propagation: Grafting named cultivars ('Li', 'Lang', 'Sugar Cane') onto seedling or sour-jujube rootstock; root suckers
grow.timeToHarvest: 1–3 years from a grafted tree
steps: Plant a grafted tree in the hottest, sunniest spot available; most varieties set fruit alone, but two varieties improve the crop.
Water for the first year, then rely on rain except in severe drought.
Remove suckers from the rootstock below the graft regularly.
Prune lightly in winter to thin crowding; fruit grows on short, deciduous branchlets each year.
Pick crisp when half to fully red for fresh eating, or leave on the tree until wrinkled to dry.

lore: The jujube is one of China's traditional 'five fruits', and jujubes and chestnuts were a bride's ritual gift in the classical rites; red dates are still scattered on wedding beds to wish couples early children — 'zǎo' sounds like 'early'. Ziziphus is also the 'lote tree' (sidr) of the Qur'an, though that is mainly Z. spina-christi.
funFact: China grows about 90% of the world's jujubes, and some trees in Shanxi are said to be over 1,000 years old.

summary: A West African evergreen, now Jamaica's national fruit, whose creamy arils are delicious — but only when the pod has opened naturally on the tree. Unripe ackee contains hypoglycin A, which causes 'Jamaican vomiting sickness' and can kill.
nativeRange: West Africa from Senegal to Gabon; introduced to Jamaica in the 18th century and grown across the Caribbean and Central America
biomes: Tropical dry forest and savanna woodland
abilities: Pods split open by themselves when ripe, revealing three arils and black seeds
Unripe arils and seeds contain hypoglycin A, which blocks fat metabolism and causes severe hypoglycaemia
Hypoglycin falls to safe levels in the arils only once the fruit opens naturally
Crushed pods and bark lather in water and were used as soap and fish poison
edibleParts: aril of naturally opened ripe fruit (boiled)
edibilityNote: Only the cream-yellow arils of fruit that has split open on the tree are eaten, after removing every seed and the pink-red membrane and boiling (discarding the water). Unripe or forced-open fruit, seeds and the membrane are poisonous and have caused many deaths.

uses.use: Leaf and bark preparations used for fever, headache and as eye drops
Leaf decoction for colds

medicinal.cautions: Unripe fruit and seeds are deadly; never force open pods.

fruit.season: Two crops: January–March and June–August in Jamaica
fruit.description: Pear-shaped, three-lobed capsule 7–10 cm, ripening from green to bright red-orange and splitting open to show three cream-yellow, brain-like arils, each capped by a glossy black seed.

seed.description: Shiny, jet-black, round to slightly oval seeds about 2–3 cm, one sitting atop each cream aril
seed.germination: Sow fresh 2–3 cm deep at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 2–4 weeks. Seeds are poisonous — handle with care

grow.water: Moderate
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained, fertile; tolerates limestone soils
grow.propagation: Seed, or grafting/air layering for earlier fruiting
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years from graft; 5–7 years from seed
steps: Sow fresh seed or plant a grafted tree in full sun, 10 m from buildings.
Water during dry spells in the first years and mulch generously.
Prune to shape and keep fruit within reach.
Never pick closed pods: wait until each pod has split open wide on the tree.
Remove the arils, discard every seed and all of the pink membrane, then boil 10–15 minutes and discard the water before cooking (e.g. with saltfish).

lore: The tree likely came to Jamaica aboard a slave ship from West Africa before 1778; it was named after Captain William Bligh, who took specimens to Kew in 1793. Ackee and saltfish is Jamaica's national dish.
funFact: The genus is named after Captain Bligh of the Bounty, who carried ackee from Jamaica to Kew Gardens.

summary: A sprawling tree from north-east Brazil whose kidney-shaped nut hangs beneath a juicy, swollen 'cashew apple'. The nut's shell holds a caustic oil related to poison ivy's urushiol, so every cashew sold must be roasted or steamed before shelling.
nativeRange: North-eastern Brazil; spread by the Portuguese to India and Africa in the 16th century; grown throughout the tropics
abilities: The true fruit is the nut; the 'apple' is a swollen flower stalk (hypocarp)
Shell oil (CNSL) is rich in anacardic acid and cardol, which blister skin
Thrives on poor sandy soils and resists drought
The Pirangi cashew tree in Brazil covers roughly 7,500–8,400 m², spreading from a single trunk
edibleParts: kernel (after roasting/steaming to remove shell oil)
cashew apple (fresh, juiced, fermented into feni)
edibilityNote: Raw cashew nuts in the shell are not safe: the shell oil causes severe burns and dermatitis, and roasting fumes irritate the lungs. 'Raw' cashews in shops have already been steamed. Cashew is a common, sometimes severe, tree-nut allergen.

uses.use: Bark tea for diarrhoea; cashew-apple juice for coughs and as a tonic
Shell oil applied to warts and corns

medicinal.cautions: Shell oil is caustic; tree-nut allergy; cross-reactivity with mango and pistachio.

fruit.season: Dry season (e.g. February–May in India and West Africa)
fruit.description: A pear-shaped, glossy red or yellow cashew apple 5–10 cm, juicy and astringent; from its tip hangs a single grey-green, kidney-shaped nut 3 cm long.

seed.description: The kernel is pale ivory, curved, kidney-shaped, about 2.5–3 cm, inside a hard grey-brown double shell filled with dark caustic oil
seed.dispersal: Bats and birds carry the apple and drop the nut
seed.germination: Sow whole nuts (in shell) fresh, 3–5 cm deep, stalk-end up, at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 2–4 weeks. Wear gloves

grow.water: Low–moderate; a dry season is needed for flowering
grow.soil: Deep sandy or lateritic soils, well-drained, pH 4.5–6.5
grow.propagation: Seed (nut), or softwood grafting of high-yielding clones
grow.timeToHarvest: 3 years from graft; 3–5 years from seed
steps: Sow nuts directly where the tree will grow (it dislikes transplanting), or plant a grafted dwarf clone.
Space 7–10 m apart in full sun; keep weeds down around young plants.
Water young trees during the first dry seasons only; mature trees need no irrigation.
Prune low branches and dead wood after harvest.
Collect fallen fruit, twist the nut from the apple, and sun-dry the nuts; roast or steam them in shells (outdoors, with gloves) before cracking.

lore: The French monk André Thevet drew the cashew in 1558, and Portuguese traders introduced it to Goa, where cashew-apple juice is distilled into the spirit feni. The Pirangi tree near Natal, Brazil, planted around 1888, is billed as the world's largest cashew.
funFact: Cashews are almost never sold in their shells, because the shell is lined with a caustic resin related to poison ivy's urushiol.

summary: A peach relative from West and Central Asia grown not for its leathery flesh but for its seed. Wild almonds are lethally bitter with amygdalin; a single mutation for sweetness, selected thousands of years ago, made almonds one of the first domesticated nut trees.
nativeRange: Western and Central Asia (Iran, Turkey, the Levant to Central Asia); cultivated in Mediterranean climates worldwide
abilities: One of the first fruit trees to bloom each year, covering hillsides in pink-white blossom in late winter
Bitter almonds contain enough amygdalin that a few dozen can kill an adult
Most cultivars are self-incompatible, so orchards depend on bees; California hires over a million beehives each February
Drought-tolerant once established
edibleParts: kernel of sweet almonds (raw, roasted, as milk, flour, marzipan)
green immature fruit (eaten whole in spring in the Middle East)
edibilityNote: Sweet almonds are safe. Bitter almonds (and wild almonds) release hydrogen cyanide; eating even small numbers raw can be fatal to children. Almond is a common tree-nut allergen.

uses.use: Soaked almonds and badam rogan (almond oil) as a brain and nerve tonic
Regular almond intake modestly lowers LDL cholesterol in trials

medicinal.cautions: Bitter almonds and bitter almond oil are poisonous; tree-nut allergy.

fruit.description: Oval, flattened, grey-green velvety drupe 3–6 cm with a thin leathery hull that dries and splits open to reveal the pitted shell.

seed.description: Teardrop-shaped, flattened kernel 2–3 cm with a cinnamon-brown, finely wrinkled skin and creamy white interior, inside a pale, pitted, tan shell
seed.germination: Cold-stratify in the shell 4–6 weeks, sow 5 cm deep; sprouts in 2–4 weeks. Seedlings may produce bitter nuts

grow.water: Low–moderate; irrigation boosts yields
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained loam, pH 6–8; intolerant of waterlogging
grow.propagation: Budding onto almond, peach or peach–almond hybrid rootstock
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–4 years
steps: Plant a self-fertile variety (e.g. 'Independence', 'Tuono', 'All-in-One') or two compatible varieties, in a frost-free, sunny site — blossom opens in late winter.
Plant bare-root in winter on well-drained ground; water deeply every 1–2 weeks in the first summer.
Prune to an open vase in the first three winters; later prune only lightly in summer to reduce disease.
Encourage bees with nearby flowers; protect blossom from late frost with fleece where practical.
Harvest when hulls split open: shake onto tarps, remove hulls and dry nuts in the sun for a week before storing.

lore: Aaron's rod miraculously budded and bore almonds in the Book of Numbers, and the Temple menorah's cups were shaped like almond blossoms. Almonds were found in Tutankhamun's tomb, and the 'almond-eyed' ideal of beauty appears in Persian poetry.
funFact: California grows around 80% of the world's almonds, and pollinating them each February takes more than half of all US commercial honeybee colonies.

summary: A majestic, long-lived nut tree from the mountains of Central Asia, prized for its oily nuts, its fine dark timber and the brown dye in its husks. Its roots and leaves release juglone, a chemical that suppresses many plants growing beneath it.
nativeRange: Mountains of Central Asia, Iran, the Caucasus, the Himalaya and south-west China; cultivated across temperate Eurasia and the Americas
abilities: Leaves, husks and roots contain juglone, an allelopathic compound that can inhibit some nearby plants, though less strongly than black walnut
Wild walnut–fruit forests of Kyrgyzstan's Arslanbob are among the largest natural walnut forests on Earth
Wind-pollinated; male and female flowers on the same tree often mature at different times
Green husks stain skin and cloth dark brown
edibleParts: nut kernel (fresh, dried, pressed for oil)
green immature nuts (pickled, or in nocino liqueur)
edibilityNote: Kernels are safe; walnut is a common tree-nut allergen. Mouldy nuts may contain mycotoxins. Husk sap stains and can irritate skin.

uses.use: Walnut kernel (hé táo rén) to tonify kidneys and lungs, ease cough and moisten the bowels
Leaf decoction (Commission E) for mild skin inflammation and excess sweating
The brain-like kernel was thought to strengthen the head and brain

medicinal.cautions: Tree-nut allergy. Husks and leaves contain juglone and can irritate skin; horse laminitis is linked mainly to bedding made from black walnut (J. nigra) shavings.

fruit.description: Round fruit 4–6 cm with a smooth, green, aromatic husk that blackens and splits, releasing a wrinkled, two-halved woody shell.

seed.description: Brain-like, wrinkled, two-lobed kernel, cream-coloured inside with a thin papery light-brown skin, about 3–4 cm across, held inside a ridged tan woody shell
seed.dispersal: Rodents, crows and jays cache and forget nuts
seed.germination: Cold-stratify in moist sand 90–120 days (or sow outdoors in autumn) 5 cm deep; protect from squirrels

grow.water: Moderate; deep watering in dry summers
grow.soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained loam, pH 6–7.5
grow.propagation: Grafting named cultivars (e.g. 'Chandler', 'Franquette', 'Broadview'); seed
grow.timeToHarvest: 4–6 years from a grafted tree; 8–12 from seed
steps: Choose a late-leafing variety where spring frosts occur, and plant where its 15–20 m canopy and juglone will not affect vegetable beds.
Plant in winter in deep soil; walnuts form long taproots and resent transplanting.
Water young trees deeply in dry spells and keep grass away from the trunk.
Prune only in late summer (bleeding sap in spring weakens the tree), removing low and crossing branches.
Gather nuts as they fall, remove husks promptly (wear gloves), and dry in shade until the kernel snaps crisply.

lore: The Romans called the walnut 'Jovis glans', acorn of Jupiter, which gave the genus name Juglans. Walnuts travelled from Persia to Greece and Rome, and Carpathian, Kashmiri and Xinjiang walnuts remain famed regional strains.
funFact: The English word 'walnut' means 'foreign nut', from Old English wealh-hnutu.

summary: A huge, long-lived tree of southern Europe and Asia Minor whose starchy nuts were the 'bread tree' staple of mountain villages from Corsica to Galicia. Individual trees live for over 2,000 years, their trunks twisting into spirals.
nativeRange: South-eastern Europe and Asia Minor; spread by the Greeks and Romans across Mediterranean and western Europe
abilities: The 'Hundred Horse Chestnut' on Mount Etna is estimated at 2,000–4,000 years old
Resprouts vigorously when coppiced, providing durable poles for centuries
Spiny burrs protect the nuts from most animals
Timber is rich in tannins, making it naturally rot-resistant
edibleParts: nuts (roasted, boiled, dried and milled into flour, candied as marrons glacés)
edibilityNote: Nuts are eaten cooked; the bitter inner skin (pellicle) is removed. Do not confuse with horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum), whose shiny conkers are toxic — sweet chestnut burrs are densely needle-spined and contain 2–3 flat-sided nuts with a tufted tip.

uses.use: Leaf infusion for whooping cough and other coughs
Sweet chestnut flower essence for despair (no pharmacological evidence)

medicinal.cautions: Do not confuse with toxic horse chestnut.

fruit.description: A green, densely spiny burr 5–10 cm that splits into four, holding usually three glossy brown nuts.

seed.description: Glossy, reddish-brown nuts 2–4 cm, rounded on one side and flat on the other, with a pale scar at the base and a tuft of hairs at the pointed tip; creamy-white starchy kernel under a bitter brown skin
seed.dispersal: Jays, squirrels, wild boar and mice cache the nuts
seed.germination: Sow fresh nuts in autumn, or stratify cold and moist for 60–90 days; plant 3–5 cm deep. Never let them dry out

grow.water: Moderate
grow.soil: Acidic, light, well-drained sandy loam (pH 4.5–6.5); does poorly on chalk or heavy clay
grow.propagation: Seed; grafting of named cultivars and hybrids (e.g. 'Marron de Lyon', 'Bouche de Bétizac')
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years from a grafted tree; 8–12 from seed
steps: Plant two or more varieties for cross-pollination, as most chestnuts are self-sterile, on acidic, free-draining ground.
Water young trees well in their first two summers and guard them against deer and rabbits.
Prune to a strong central leader in early years; older trees need little pruning (or coppice on a 12–20 year cycle for poles).
Watch for chestnut blight and gall wasp in affected regions, and buy resistant stock.
Gather nuts from the ground daily as burrs drop; score each nut before roasting so it doesn't explode, or dry and mill for flour.

lore: Xenophon described Greek soldiers eating chestnuts in Asia Minor around 400 BCE, and in Corsica and the Cévennes chestnut flour ('farina di castagne') sustained villages so fully that the tree was called 'l'arbre à pain', the bread tree.
funFact: The 'Hundred Horse Chestnut' on Mount Etna got its name from a legend that it sheltered a queen and her hundred knights from a storm.

summary: A tough desert tree of Central Asia, related to cashew and mango, whose nut shells split open as they ripen — the 'smiling nut' of Iran and 'happy nut' of China. Wild stands in Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Afghanistan are declining and assessed Near Threatened.
nativeRange: Central Asia: north-east Iran, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan and Kyrgyzstan; cultivated in Iran, Turkey, the US, Syria and the Mediterranean
abilities: Survives summer heat above 40 °C and winter cold below −20 °C
Tolerates saline irrigation water better than most nut crops
Dioecious and wind-pollinated: one male tree serves about 8–10 females
Bears in alternate heavy and light years
edibleParts: kernel (raw, roasted, in sweets like baklava)
edibilityNote: Kernels are safe; pistachio is a tree-nut allergen and cross-reacts with cashew. Poorly stored or damaged nuts can carry aflatoxin, and bulk-stored nuts can self-heat and ignite.

uses.use: Nuts as a tonic for the heart, liver and brain; resin of related species (mastic) for the stomach
Pistachio intake associated in trials with improved blood lipids

medicinal.cautions: Tree-nut allergy (cashew cross-reactivity); aflatoxin risk in damaged nuts.

fruit.description: Oval drupe 2–2.5 cm in grape-like clusters, with a thin rosy-pink to red-tinged hull over a cream, hard shell that splits along its seam when ripe.

seed.description: Elongated, green to yellow-green kernel 1.5–2 cm with a thin purplish-red papery skin, inside a smooth beige shell that gapes open
seed.germination: Remove shell, soak 24 hours, cold-stratify 4–6 weeks, sow at 20–25 °C; 1–3 weeks

grow.water: Low; deep, infrequent irrigation improves yield
grow.soil: Deep, very well-drained sandy loam; tolerates alkaline and saline soils, pH 7–8
grow.propagation: Budding female cultivars ('Kerman', 'Ahmad Aghaei') and males ('Peters') onto P. atlantica, P. integerrima or UCB-1 rootstock
grow.timeToHarvest: 5–7 years; full production at 15–20 years
steps: Check that you have long, hot, dry summers (pistachios need heat to ripen) and at least 800 chill hours in winter.
Plant one male tree for every 8–10 females, upwind, in deep, perfectly drained soil.
Water deeply but rarely; mature trees need little water but crop better with irrigation.
Train to an open vase in the first years, then prune lightly in winter.
Shake ripe nuts from the tree when hulls slip easily from the shells, hull and dry within 24 hours to prevent staining and mould.

lore: Pistachios were found at the Neolithic site of Jarmo in Iraq, about 6750 BCE, and legend says the Queen of Sheba reserved them for herself and her court. Iran's Rafsanjan region has been a famed pistachio centre for centuries.
funFact: Large stockpiles of pistachios can self-heat and even spontaneously combust, so shippers treat them as a fire risk in cargo holds.

summary: Bread wheat is a hexaploid hybrid of three wild grasses, formed when cultivated emmer crossed with goatgrass near the Caspian about 9,000 years ago. Grown on more land than any other crop, it supplies about a fifth of all calories humans eat.
nativeRange: Of cultivated origin in the Fertile Crescent and south-west of the Caspian (Transcaucasia/northern Iran); grown on every continent except Antarctica
abilities: Hexaploid: carries three complete genomes (A, B and D) from three ancestral species
Gluten proteins form an elastic network that traps gas, letting dough rise
Domestic wheat lost the 'shattering' trait, so ripe grain stays on the ear until harvested
Winter wheat needs cold vernalisation before it will flower
edibilityNote: Grain is a staple. Gluten triggers coeliac disease in about 1% of people; wheat is also a common allergen. Grain infected with ergot fungus is toxic.

uses.use: Wheat porridges for convalescents and bran poultices
Wheat bran as a bulk-forming laxative with good trial evidence for constipation

medicinal.cautions: Coeliac disease, wheat allergy and non-coeliac gluten sensitivity.

fruit.season: Early to midsummer (winter wheat); late summer (spring wheat)
fruit.description: Dense ear (spike) of 30–60 grains arranged in spikelets, golden when ripe, awned or awnless.

seed.description: Oval to egg-shaped grain 5–7 mm, with a deep crease along one side and a tuft of fine hairs at the tip; red-brown, amber or white, hard and glassy or soft and floury
seed.germination: Sow 2.5–4 cm deep at 4–25 °C; emerges in 5–10 days. Winter varieties need weeks of cold to flower

grow.zones: Annual crop: winter wheat in USDA 3–8; spring wheat in short-summer regions
grow.water: Moderate (300–900 mm over the season)
grow.soil: Well-drained loam or clay loam, pH 6–7.5
grow.propagation: Seed
grow.timeToHarvest: Winter wheat 8–10 months; spring wheat 90–120 days
steps: Prepare a fine, firm seedbed; sow winter wheat in autumn or spring wheat as early as the soil can be worked, about 2.5–4 cm deep in rows 15–20 cm apart (or broadcast and rake in).
Keep weeds down in the first weeks; a small plot can be hoed between rows.
Feed with nitrogen (compost or fertiliser) in early spring as the plants begin to stretch.
Harvest when the straw is golden and a grain dented with a thumbnail is hard; cut and bundle stems into sheaves to dry for a week.
Thresh by beating sheaves in a sack or on a tarp, then winnow in a breeze to blow away the chaff.

lore: Wheat was one of the 'founder crops' of Neolithic agriculture at sites like Abu Hureyra and Göbekli Tepe's region, and Egyptian tombs held bread loaves for the afterlife. In the Lord's Prayer and the Eucharist, wheaten bread became the central Christian symbol of sustenance.
funFact: The bread-wheat genome is about five times larger than the human genome.

summary: The grain that feeds more than half of humanity, domesticated from wild Oryza rufipogon in the Yangtze valley about 9,000 years ago. Rice can grow in standing water because hollow channels in its stems pipe air down to its roots.
nativeRange: Domesticated in the Yangtze valley of China (japonica) and later hybridised in South Asia (indica); grown in tropical and warm-temperate regions worldwide
abilities: Aerenchyma tissue carries oxygen from leaves to roots in flooded soil
Some varieties carry the Sub1 gene, letting them survive two weeks fully underwater
Paddy fields support fish, frogs and ducks in traditional integrated systems
The International Rice Genebank in the Philippines holds over 130,000 rice accessions
edibleParts: fermented into wine, vinegar and sake
edibilityNote: Cooked grain is safe. Rice can accumulate inorganic arsenic from soil and water; rinsing and cooking in excess water reduces it. Cooked rice left warm can grow Bacillus cereus.

uses.use: Rice congee as a gentle food to strengthen digestion; red yeast rice (fermented with Monascus) for blood circulation
Rice-based oral rehydration solutions for diarrhoea
Navara rice used in Kerala's 'Njavarakizhi' massage therapy

medicinal.cautions: Arsenic in rice products, especially for infants. Red yeast rice contains lovastatin and shares statin side effects.

fruit.season: Late summer to autumn in temperate zones; multiple crops a year in the tropics
fruit.description: Drooping panicle of 50–500 spikelets, each enclosing a single grain in a tough, ridged, straw-coloured husk (hull).

seed.description: Paddy grain is oblong, 5–10 mm, enclosed in a golden, ridged, sometimes awned hull; dehulled brown rice is smooth, slim to round and tan, red or black, with a white starchy interior
seed.dispersal: Humans; wild relatives shatter and float on water
seed.germination: Soak 24 hours, keep moist and warm (25–35 °C); sprouts in 2–4 days

grow.zones: Annual warm-season crop; needs 3–6 frost-free months above about 20 °C
grow.water: Very high (paddy) or high rainfall (upland rice)
grow.soil: Heavy clay or silt that holds water; pH 5–7
grow.propagation: Seed, direct-sown or transplanted as seedlings
grow.timeToHarvest: 100–180 days depending on variety
steps: Soak seed for a day and sow thickly in a moist nursery bed or trays.
After 3–4 weeks, transplant seedlings in clumps of 2–3, about 20 cm apart, into a levelled, puddled (muddy) bed or tub.
Keep 5–10 cm of standing water over the soil through growth to suppress weeds; drain briefly mid-season to strengthen roots.
Drain the field 2–3 weeks before harvest, when panicles droop and grains turn golden.
Cut, dry the sheaves, thresh, then dry grain to about 14% moisture before hulling.

lore: In Japan, the emperor ritually plants and harvests rice in the palace paddies, and Shinto's Inari is the god of rice. The Ifugao rice terraces of the Philippines, a UNESCO World Heritage site, are popularly said to be 2,000 years old, though radiocarbon studies suggest many were built in the last 400 years or so.
funFact: The 1966 'miracle rice' IR8 from the International Rice Research Institute roughly doubled yields across Asia and averted predicted famines.

summary: Bred about 9,000 years ago in Mexico's Balsas River valley from teosinte, a wild grass with tiny, rock-hard seeds. Maize is now the world's most-produced grain by weight and cannot survive without people, since its kernels never fall free of the cob.
nativeRange: Domesticated in south-western Mexico (Balsas valley) from Zea mays subsp. parviglumis; grown worldwide
abilities: C4 photosynthesis makes it one of the most productive crops in heat and strong light
Each silk is a pollen tube channel leading to one kernel
Kernels remain locked on the cob, so maize depends entirely on humans to sow it
Grown in the 'Three Sisters' polyculture: beans climb maize stalks and squash shades the soil
edibilityNote: Safe when cooked. A diet dependent on untreated maize causes pellagra (niacin deficiency); nixtamalisation with lime, as practised in Mesoamerica, prevents it. Mouldy maize may carry aflatoxins.

uses.use: Corn silk (yù mǐ xū) as a diuretic for oedema and urinary complaints
Corn-silk tea and atole (maize gruel) for the sick and nursing mothers

medicinal.cautions: Pellagra risk where maize is the main food and is not nixtamalised.

fruit.description: Female inflorescence (ear) 15–30 cm wrapped in green husks with silky threads, bearing 8–24 rows of kernels on a central cob.

seed.description: Wedge- to tooth-shaped kernels 8–12 mm, smooth and glossy; yellow, white, red, blue-purple or multicoloured; dent types show a dimple on top, flint types are round and hard
seed.germination: Sow 3–5 cm deep once soil exceeds 10–12 °C; emerges in 5–10 days

grow.zones: Annual warm-season crop; frost-free season of 70–120+ days
grow.water: Moderate–high, especially at tasselling and silking
grow.soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained loam, pH 5.8–7
grow.propagation: Seed
grow.timeToHarvest: Sweetcorn 65–100 days; grain maize 90–150 days
steps: After the last frost, sow seeds 3–5 cm deep, 25–30 cm apart, in a block of at least four short rows rather than one long row — maize is wind-pollinated.
Feed generously (it is a heavy nitrogen feeder) and keep weeds down while young; or interplant with climbing beans and squash in the Three Sisters pattern.
Water deeply when tassels and silks appear; drought then leaves gaps on the cob.
Pick sweetcorn about three weeks after silking, when silks are brown and a pierced kernel gives milky juice.
For dry grain or popcorn, leave cobs on the plant until husks are papery, then dry further indoors and shell.

lore: In the K'iche' Maya Popol Vuh, the gods finally made true humans out of maize dough after failed attempts with mud and wood. The Aztec honoured maize deities such as Centeotl and Chicomecōātl.
funFact: Maize cobs about 6,250 years old from Guilá Naquitz cave in Oaxaca are tiny — one is only about 2.5 cm long.

summary: Domesticated around Lake Titicaca 7,000–10,000 years ago, the potato is the world's leading non-grain staple. Andean farmers still grow thousands of varieties, and freeze-dry them into chuño that keeps for years.
nativeRange: Andes of southern Peru and north-west Bolivia; also Chilean lowlands; grown worldwide
abilities: Stores energy in underground stem tubers that can each sprout a new plant
Over 4,000 varieties are known in the Andes
Tubers turn green and produce toxic glycoalkaloids when exposed to light
Cold storage converts starch to sugar, which is why chilled potatoes taste sweet
edibilityNote: Tubers are eaten cooked. Leaves, stems, berries, sprouts and green-skinned or sprouting tubers contain solanine and chaconine, which cause vomiting and neurological symptoms; cut away all green parts and sprouts.

uses.use: Raw grated potato poultices on burns, bruises and swollen eyes
Slices applied to the temples for headache and fever

medicinal.cautions: Green tubers, sprouts and all aerial parts are toxic.

fruit.description: Small, green, tomato-like berry 1–4 cm, poisonous, holding up to 300 seeds.

seed.description: 'True potato seed' is tiny, flat, kidney-shaped, cream to pale-yellow, about 1.5–2 mm; growers instead plant 'seed potatoes' — small whole tubers or chunks with eyes
seed.dispersal: Tubers spread vegetatively; berries by animals
seed.germination: True seed: sow on the surface at 15–20 °C; 1–2 weeks. Seed potatoes: chit (pre-sprout) in light for 4–6 weeks

grow.zones: Annual cool-season crop; grown in USDA 3–10 by adjusting planting time
grow.water: Moderate–high, steady, especially while tubers form
grow.soil: Loose, deep, slightly acidic (pH 5–6.5), well-drained; acidity reduces scab
grow.propagation: Certified seed potatoes (tubers)
grow.timeToHarvest: Early 'new' potatoes 60–90 days; main crop 100–140 days
steps: Set certified seed potatoes in egg cartons in a bright, cool room 4–6 weeks before planting to grow short, sturdy sprouts.
Plant 10–15 cm deep, 30 cm apart in rows 60–75 cm apart, once soil reaches about 7 °C and frost risk is passing.
'Earth up' by drawing soil over stems as they grow, leaving only the top leaves showing — this keeps tubers covered and prevents greening.
Water regularly once flowers appear; watch for late blight (brown leaf patches in warm, wet weather) and remove infected foliage.
Dig new potatoes when plants flower; for storage, cut down foliage when it yellows, wait two weeks, then lift and cure tubers in the dark.

lore: Spanish conquistadors brought tubers to Europe around 1570. Ireland's dependence on a few varieties led to the Great Famine of 1845–52, when late blight killed about a million people.
funFact: In 1995 the potato became the first vegetable grown in space, aboard the shuttle Columbia.

summary: A sprawling Andean nightshade, domesticated in Mexico, that Europeans long feared as poisonous before it conquered Italian and then world cuisine. Its pea-sized wild ancestor still grows in coastal Ecuador and Peru.
nativeRange: Wild ancestor (Solanum pimpinellifolium) in coastal Ecuador and Peru; domesticated in Mesoamerica; grown worldwide
abilities: Flowers are buzz-pollinated: bumblebees vibrate them to release pollen
Glandular hairs on stems release the distinctive 'tomato' smell and trap small insects
Fruit ripening is triggered by the plant hormone ethylene
Stems lying on soil sprout roots along their length
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is safe. Leaves and stems contain tomatine and other glycoalkaloids and are mildly toxic, especially to pets; green fruit has small amounts that are usually harmless when cooked.

uses.use: Fruit and leaves applied to skin infections and sore throats
Lycopene from cooked tomatoes studied for prostate and cardiovascular health, with mixed results

medicinal.cautions: Leaves and stems are toxic to pets; tomatoes can worsen reflux.

fruit.description: Juicy berry 1–15 cm, round, oval, plum- or heart-shaped; red, yellow, orange, pink, green-striped or near-black; fleshy walls around gel-filled seed chambers.

seed.description: Flat, round to kidney-shaped, pale tan to buff seeds about 3 mm across, covered in fine silky hairs and coated in jelly in the fruit
seed.dispersal: Birds, tortoises (in the Galápagos) and mammals
seed.germination: Sow 0.5 cm deep at 20–28 °C; sprouts in 5–10 days. Ferment saved seed in its jelly for 2–3 days, then rinse and dry

grow.zones: Annual warm-season crop; frost-tender perennial in USDA 10–12
grow.water: Moderate, steady; irregular watering causes splitting and blossom-end rot
grow.soil: Rich, well-drained loam, pH 6–7
grow.propagation: Seed; side-shoot cuttings root in water
grow.timeToHarvest: 60–100 days from transplanting
steps: Sow indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost; pot on seedlings when they have true leaves.
After frost, harden off and plant deeply — bury the stem up to the first leaves, as it will root along its length.
Stake or cage plants; on cordon (indeterminate) varieties, pinch out side shoots in leaf axils.
Water deeply at the base and mulch to keep moisture even; feed with a high-potassium fertiliser once fruit sets.
Pick when fully coloured; at season's end, ripen green fruit indoors in a bag with a banana.

lore: The Italian herbalist Pietro Andrea Mattioli called it 'pomi d'oro' (golden apples) in 1544, and Europeans grew it as an ornamental for decades fearing it was poisonous. The Spanish town of Buñol throws well over 100 tonnes of tomatoes each August at La Tomatina.
funFact: In 1893 the US Supreme Court ruled (Nix v. Hedden) that the tomato is legally a vegetable, though botanically a fruit.

summary: The species behind bell peppers, jalapeños, cayenne, paprika and most chillies, domesticated in Mexico over 6,000 years ago. Its fiery capsaicin deters mammals while birds, which lack the pain receptor it triggers, eat the fruit and spread its seeds.
nativeRange: Southern North America to northern South America, domesticated in central-east Mexico; grown worldwide
abilities: Capsaicin binds the TRPV1 heat-pain receptor in mammals but not in birds
Capsaicin also protects seeds from Fusarium fungal attack
Heat is concentrated in the pale placental tissue, not the seeds themselves
Spread from the Americas to India, China and Africa within a century of 1492
edibleParts: leaves (cooked, in Filipino tinola and Korean dishes)
edibilityNote: Fruit is safe; very hot types can burn skin, eyes and the gut. Wash hands after cutting chillies.

uses.use: Chilli used for toothache, cough and to treat infections, recorded in the Florentine Codex
High-strength capsaicin patches (Qutenza) are approved for nerve pain after shingles; low-dose creams for arthritis pain

medicinal.cautions: Irritant to skin, eyes and mucous membranes; may aggravate reflux and haemorrhoids.

fruit.description: Hollow berry ranging from pea-sized wild chiltepins to 15 cm bell peppers; green ripening to red, yellow, orange, purple or brown; seeds attached to a pale central placenta.

seed.description: Flat, kidney- to disc-shaped, cream to pale-yellow seeds about 3–5 mm, smooth, clustered on the placenta
seed.germination: Sow 0.5 cm deep at 25–30 °C (bottom heat helps); sprouts in 7–21 days

grow.zones: Annual in temperate zones; short-lived perennial in USDA 10–12
grow.water: Moderate; let the surface dry slightly between waterings
grow.soil: Fertile, well-drained loam, pH 6–7
grow.propagation: Seed; cuttings
grow.timeToHarvest: 60–90 days from transplanting (longer for very hot types)
steps: Sow indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost on a warm mat; chillies need warmth to germinate.
Transplant after night temperatures stay above 12 °C, 40–50 cm apart; pots of 10+ litres work well.
Water evenly, mulch and feed with a potassium-rich fertiliser once flowers appear; pinch the first flowers on small plants to build size.
Stake heavy-cropping plants; slight dryness near ripening increases heat.
Snip fruit with scissors when green or fully coloured; dry on strings (ristras) or freeze. Overwinter plants indoors to crop earlier next year.

lore: Columbus called chillies 'pimiento', mistaking them for relatives of black pepper, and Portuguese traders carried them to Goa, Bengal and Africa within decades. Today India is the world's largest producer, and the chilli is inseparable from Sichuan, Thai and Korean food.
funFact: Wild chiltepin, the ancestral chilli, is the official native spice of Texas.

summary: A woody shrub from the southern Amazon whose starchy roots feed over half a billion people, mainly in Africa. Every part contains cyanogenic glucosides, and Indigenous Amazonians developed elaborate grating, pressing and fermenting methods to make it safe — techniques later adopted across Africa and Asia.
nativeRange: Southern Amazon basin of Brazil (Rondônia/Mato Grosso); grown throughout the tropics
abilities: Survives drought, poor acidic soils and erratic rainfall where grains fail
Roots can be left in the ground for up to two years and harvested when needed
Contains linamarin and lotaustralin, which release hydrogen cyanide when cells are damaged
Grown easily from stem cuttings
edibleParts: roots (peeled, soaked, fermented, cooked — as fufu, gari, farinha, tapioca)
young leaves (pounded and long-boiled, e.g. pondu, saka-saka)
edibilityNote: Never eat raw. Roots and leaves release cyanide; 'sweet' varieties need peeling and thorough cooking, while 'bitter' varieties must be grated, soaked or fermented, pressed and cooked. Poorly processed cassava causes acute poisoning and the paralytic disease konzo.

uses.use: Leaf poultices applied to wounds and sores
Tapioca porridge as a gentle food for diarrhoea

medicinal.cautions: Cyanogenic: inadequately processed roots and leaves are poisonous; chronic exposure linked to konzo and tropical ataxic neuropathy.

fruit.description: Rounded, six-winged green capsule about 1.5 cm that dries and splits explosively, throwing out three seeds.

seed.description: Oval, smooth, mottled grey-brown seeds about 1 cm long, with a pale fleshy appendage (caruncle) at one end
seed.dispersal: Explosive capsules; ants carry seeds by the caruncle
seed.germination: Seed used mainly in breeding; needs warmth (30–35 °C). Farmers plant stem cuttings

grow.zones: Tropical only (USDA 10–12); annual in warm subtropics
grow.water: Low–moderate; very drought-tolerant once established
grow.soil: Light, sandy or loamy, well-drained; tolerates poor acidic soils (pH 4.5–7)
grow.propagation: Stem cuttings 20–30 cm long from mature, disease-free stems
grow.timeToHarvest: 8–24 months (sweet types from 6–8 months)
steps: Cut 20–30 cm lengths with 5–8 nodes from mature, virus-free stems (check for mosaic disease).
Plant at the start of rains, 1 m apart, either upright, angled or flat with two-thirds buried and buds pointing up.
Weed for the first three months, after which the canopy shades out weeds.
Harvest by lifting the stem and pulling roots; process within 1–2 days as roots spoil quickly.
Peel, then soak, grate, ferment, press and cook as appropriate to the variety before eating — never eat raw.

lore: The Tupi and Arawak peoples grew cassava long before European contact, inventing the woven tipiti press to squeeze out its poisonous juice. Portuguese traders carried it from Brazil to the Congo basin in the 16th century, where it became central to Central African cuisine.
funFact: The 'pearls' in bubble tea are made from tapioca, the purified starch of cassava roots.

summary: A heat- and drought-hardy grain domesticated in the eastern Sahel of Sudan around 5,000–6,000 years ago, and the fifth most important cereal in the world. It feeds hundreds of millions across Africa and India, and its stalks give sugar syrup, broom straw and fodder.
nativeRange: North-east Africa (Sudan, Ethiopia and the eastern Sahel); grown in semi-arid regions worldwide
abilities: C4 photosynthesis and a waxy leaf bloom let it yield where maize fails in heat and drought
Can go dormant in drought and resume growing when rain returns
Roots exude sorgoleone, a compound that suppresses nearby weeds
Young plants and regrowth contain dhurrin, which releases cyanide
edibleParts: grain (flour for roti, injera-style flatbreads, porridge, couscous; brewed into beer)
edibilityNote: Grain is safe and gluten-free. Young leaves, shoots and frost- or drought-stressed regrowth contain dhurrin, which can poison grazing livestock with cyanide.

uses.use: Red leaf-sheath extract (from dye sorghum) as a blood tonic for anaemia
Jowar as a light, cooling grain for digestive and urinary complaints

medicinal.cautions: Forage is cyanogenic to livestock, especially young or stressed regrowth.

fruit.season: End of the rainy season / late summer–autumn
fruit.description: Compact or open panicle (head) at the top of a stalk 1–4 m tall, bearing hundreds of round grains.

seed.description: Round to slightly oval grains 3–5 mm, white, cream, yellow, red, brown or near-black, often partly enclosed in papery glumes
seed.germination: Sow 2–4 cm deep once soil exceeds about 15 °C; emerges in 4–10 days

grow.water: Low–moderate (400–600 mm per season)
grow.soil: Tolerates poor, sandy, clay or slightly saline soils, pH 5.5–8.5
grow.propagation: Seed
grow.timeToHarvest: 90–130 days
steps: Sow in warm soil after the rains start or after frost, 2–4 cm deep, 15–20 cm apart in rows 60–75 cm apart.
Thin seedlings and weed in the first month; little care is needed afterwards.
Water only in prolonged drought; avoid grazing animals on young or stressed plants.
Protect ripening heads from birds with netting or paper bags.
Cut heads when the grain is hard and can't be dented with a fingernail, dry them, then thresh by beating.

lore: Sorghum grains impressed into pottery at Kassala in Sudan are among the earliest evidence of its domestication. In China, sorghum is distilled into baijiu spirits such as Moutai, and the novel and film 'Red Sorghum' made its fields an icon of rural China.
funFact: Sorghum stalks can also be pressed for sweet juice: 'sorghum molasses' was a staple sweetener in the 19th-century American South.

summary: A goosefoot domesticated around Lake Titicaca about 5,000–7,000 years ago, quinoa is not a grass but a 'pseudocereal' related to spinach and beet. It grows at nearly 4,000 m on salty, frosty altiplano soils and its seeds are a complete protein.
nativeRange: Andes of Bolivia and Peru (Lake Titicaca basin), also lowland Chile; now grown in many countries
abilities: Tolerates soil salinity close to that of seawater in some varieties
Survives frost, drought and intense UV at high altitude
Leaves have bladder-like hairs that store salt away from tissues
Seed coats are covered in bitter saponins that deter birds and insects
edibilityNote: Seeds must be rinsed or scrubbed to remove bitter saponins, which irritate the gut. Leaves contain oxalates; eat cooked and in moderation.

uses.use: Seed and leaf poultices for bruises, fractures and inflammation; saponin-rich wash water as soap

compounds: complete protein (all essential amino acids, rich in lysine)
medicinal.cautions: Rinse well to remove saponins; leaves high in oxalate.

fruit.season: Late summer to autumn (5–6 months after sowing)
fruit.description: Large dense seedheads 15–70 cm on stems 1–2 m tall, ripening red, purple, orange, yellow or cream.

seed.description: Small, flattened disc-shaped seeds 1.5–2.5 mm, white, cream, red or black, with a visible pale ring (the embryo) around the edge, coated in a powdery bitter saponin layer
seed.germination: Very fast: sow shallow (1 cm) in cool soil at 5–20 °C; sprouts in 1–4 days, even in a dish of water

grow.zones: Annual; best in regions where summer days stay below about 32 °C
grow.water: Low–moderate
grow.soil: Well-drained, tolerates poor, sandy and saline soils, pH 6–8.5
grow.propagation: Seed
grow.timeToHarvest: 90–150 days
steps: Sow in spring when soil reaches about 7–10 °C, 1 cm deep, in rows 40–50 cm apart; thin to 15–20 cm.
Weed carefully in early weeks — seedlings look like the weed lamb's quarters, its close relative.
Water lightly; heavy watering and humid heat (over 32 °C) at flowering cause pollen sterility.
Harvest when leaves drop and seeds can be rubbed out of the head with a fingernail, before autumn rain.
Dry heads fully, rub over a screen, winnow, and wash seeds repeatedly in water until no foam forms.

lore: The Inca called quinoa 'chisiya mama', mother of all grains, and the emperor is said to have sown the first seeds of each season with a golden tool. Spanish colonists discouraged its cultivation because of its role in Andean rituals.
funFact: The United Nations declared 2013 the International Year of Quinoa.

summary: Domesticated in north-east China from wild Glycine soja around 9,000–5,000 years ago, soybean is now one of the world's most important protein and oil crops, mostly fed to livestock. Its seeds are about 36–40% protein and 18–20% oil.
nativeRange: North-east and central China; grown worldwide, especially in Brazil, the United States, Argentina and India
abilities: Root nodules host Bradyrhizobium bacteria that fix nitrogen from the air
Flowering is triggered by shortening day length (photoperiod sensitive)
Seeds contain isoflavones that mimic oestrogen weakly
Raw beans contain trypsin inhibitors that block protein digestion until cooked
edibleParts: seeds (cooked, as tofu, soy milk, miso, tempeh, natto, soy sauce)
edibilityNote: Beans must be cooked or fermented; raw soybeans contain trypsin inhibitors and lectins that cause digestive upset. Soy is one of the major food allergens.

uses.use: Fermented black soybean (dàn dòu chǐ) for colds and restlessness
Soy protein modestly lowers LDL cholesterol; isoflavones studied for menopausal hot flushes

medicinal.cautions: Soy allergy. Large doses of isoflavone supplements are not advised with hormone-sensitive cancers without medical advice; may affect thyroid medication absorption.

fruit.description: Hairy, slightly curved pods 3–8 cm in clusters, green maturing to tan or brown, each with 2–4 seeds.

seed.description: Round to oval beans 5–11 mm, smooth, most commonly pale yellow-cream with a small dark or light hilum (scar), but also green, brown, black or mottled
seed.dispersal: Pods split on drying (wild forms more strongly)
seed.germination: Sow 2.5–4 cm deep in warm soil (above 15 °C); emerges in 5–10 days. Inoculate seed with Bradyrhizobium where soy is new

grow.zones: Annual warm-season crop; choose maturity group for your latitude
grow.water: Moderate; most critical at flowering and pod fill
grow.soil: Well-drained loam, pH 6–7
grow.propagation: Seed
grow.timeToHarvest: Edamame 75–90 days; dry beans 100–150 days
steps: After the last frost, when soil is warm, dust seed with soybean inoculant and sow 3 cm deep, 5–8 cm apart, in rows 40–75 cm apart.
Keep weed-free for the first 6 weeks; no nitrogen fertiliser is needed once nodules form.
Water during flowering and pod fill if dry.
For edamame, pick when pods are plump and bright green; boil in salted water.
For dry beans, harvest when pods are brown and rattle, before they split; thresh and dry to below 13% moisture.

lore: Chinese tradition counts soy among the 'five sacred grains', and tofu is credited (doubtfully) to Liu An, prince of Huainan, in the 2nd century BCE. Benjamin Franklin sent soybeans from London to America in 1770.
funFact: Henry Ford had a car body built from soybean-based plastic in 1941 and wore a suit made of soy fibre.

summary: One of the Neolithic 'founder crops' of the Fertile Crescent, gathered and grown for over 9,000 years. Its flat, lens-shaped seed literally gave its name to the optical lens. iNaturalist now places it in Vicia.
nativeRange: Fertile Crescent (Turkey, Syria, Iraq, Israel); domesticated from wild Vicia orientalis; grown widely in South Asia, the Middle East, Canada and Australia
abilities: Fixes nitrogen through root nodules with Rhizobium leguminosarum
Grows on minimal water in cool seasons
Cooks quickly without soaking, unlike most dry pulses
Seeds contain about 25% protein
edibleParts: seeds (cooked whole or split as dal, soups)
edibilityNote: Seeds are eaten cooked. Raw lentils contain lectins; always cook.

uses.use: Lentil decoctions and poultices for skin sores and digestive complaints
Pulses including lentils lower post-meal blood sugar and LDL cholesterol in trials

medicinal.cautions: Raw lentils contain lectins; flatulence common.

fruit.description: Short, flat, oblong pods 1–2 cm, holding 1–2 seeds, on a slender bushy plant 30–50 cm tall.

seed.description: Flat, round, biconvex, lens-shaped seeds 3–8 mm across; seed coat green, brown, grey, tan, black or speckled, with orange, red, yellow or green interior when split
seed.dispersal: Humans (pods of domesticated forms do not split readily)
seed.germination: Sow 2–5 cm deep into cool soil (from 5 °C); emerges in 7–10 days

grow.zones: Annual cool-season crop; spring sowing in cold regions, winter crop in subtropics (e.g. India's rabi season)
grow.water: Low
grow.soil: Well-drained loam, pH 6–8; dislikes waterlogging
grow.propagation: Seed
grow.timeToHarvest: 80–110 days
steps: Sow in early spring (or autumn in mild regions) 2–4 cm deep, about 2–5 cm apart in rows 20–30 cm apart; inoculate seed if lentils are new to the soil.
Keep weeds down early, as lentil seedlings compete poorly.
Water only if very dry; too much water encourages disease.
Harvest when lower pods turn brown and rattle; pull whole plants and dry them on a sheet.
Thresh by trampling or beating, winnow, and store dried seeds in airtight jars.

lore: In Genesis, Esau sold his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of red lentil stew. Lentils have been found in Egyptian tombs, and in Italy they are eaten on New Year's Eve for prosperity, their shape recalling coins.
funFact: The word 'lens' comes from the Latin for lentil, because early convex glass lenses were the same shape as the seed.

summary: A small, hairy-leaved legume domesticated in south-east Turkey about 10,000 years ago and the base of hummus, falafel, chana masala and besan flour. India grows about 70% of the world's crop.
nativeRange: South-eastern Turkey (wild ancestor Cicer reticulatum); grown across South Asia, the Middle East, the Mediterranean, Ethiopia, Australia and the Americas
abilities: Leaf hairs secrete malic and oxalic acid, deterring insects (dew on leaves is sour)
Deep taproot lets it mature on stored soil moisture after rains end
Fixes nitrogen through root nodules
Two main types: small, dark, angular 'desi' and large, cream 'kabuli'
edibleParts: seeds (cooked, roasted, ground into besan/gram flour)
edibilityNote: Dry seeds must be soaked and cooked. Raw dry chickpeas are indigestible and contain antinutrients.

uses.use: Chickpea broth as a diuretic and for kidney stones
Besan paste (with turmeric) as a skin cleanser (ubtan)
Chickpeas as a diuretic and to promote menstruation

medicinal.cautions: Legume allergy (cross-reaction with peanut and lentil reported).

fruit.season: Spring to early summer (winter crop in India)
fruit.description: Short, inflated, hairy pods 2–3 cm, like small balloons, usually holding 1–2 seeds.

seed.description: Round to angular seeds with a pointed beak like a ram's head: kabuli types cream-beige, smooth, 8–12 mm; desi types smaller, wrinkled, brown, green or black, 5–8 mm
seed.germination: Sow 4–8 cm deep in soil above about 10 °C; emerges in 7–14 days

grow.zones: Annual cool-season crop (spring in temperate areas, winter in subtropics)
grow.water: Low; grows on residual soil moisture
grow.soil: Well-drained loam or clay loam, pH 6–8; intolerant of waterlogging
grow.propagation: Seed
grow.timeToHarvest: 90–120 days for dry seed
steps: Sow seed 4–8 cm deep after the last hard frost (or in autumn in mild-winter areas), 8–10 cm apart in rows 30–45 cm apart.
Do not fertilise with nitrogen; inoculate seed with Mesorhizobium ciceri if chickpeas haven't grown there before.
Water sparingly — damp conditions encourage Ascochyta blight.
Pick some green pods to eat fresh, or wait until plants turn yellow-brown and pods rattle.
Pull or cut plants, dry, thresh and store seed dry; soak overnight before cooking.

lore: The Roman orator Cicero's family name is said to come from 'cicer', chickpea, perhaps after a wart on an ancestor's nose. Roasted chickpeas were sold as street food in ancient Rome and are still the 'leblebi' of Turkey.
funFact: During coffee shortages in Europe, roasted ground chickpeas were brewed as a coffee substitute.

summary: A giant perennial grass domesticated in New Guinea about 8,000 years ago whose stems store sucrose at up to 20% of their weight. Its spread shaped world history — from Indian sugar crystallisation in the Gupta era to the Atlantic slave trade and Caribbean plantations.
nativeRange: New Guinea (derived from Saccharum robustum); modern canes are hybrids with S. spontaneum; grown throughout the tropics and subtropics
abilities: C4 photosynthesis makes it one of the most efficient converters of sunlight into biomass
Stems store sucrose at up to about 20% of fresh weight
Grows 3–6 m tall and regrows from the stubble ('ratoon') for several harvests
Crushed fibre (bagasse) fuels the mills that process it
edibleParts: stem juice (fresh, boiled into jaggery, panela, sugar, molasses, fermented to rum)
edibilityNote: Juice and chewed stems are safe. Refined sugar in excess is linked to tooth decay, obesity and type 2 diabetes.

uses.use: Fresh cane juice and jaggery (guḍa) as a cooling tonic and for jaundice; jaggery as the sweet base of many remedies
Policosanol from cane wax developed as a cholesterol-lowering drug (later trials outside Cuba were negative)

medicinal.cautions: Sugar overconsumption; stem edges and leaves are sharp.

fruit.season: Flowers in the short days of late autumn–winter in the tropics (rarely sets seed)
fruit.description: A large, silky, silvery-plumed panicle (arrow) up to 1 m long; most commercial canes rarely set seed.

seed.description: Minute, brown, oblong grains about 1–1.5 mm, enclosed in fluffy hairy spikelets; produced mostly in breeding stations
seed.germination: Breeding only: surface-sow fuzz at 30 °C under high humidity; farmers plant stem cuttings ('setts')

grow.water: High (1,500–2,500 mm over the season)
grow.soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained loam, pH 6–7.5
grow.propagation: Stem cuttings (setts) of 2–3 nodes
grow.timeToHarvest: 10–18 months; ratoon crops each year after
steps: Cut mature, healthy canes into setts of 2–3 nodes (buds).
Lay setts horizontally in furrows 10–15 cm deep, 1–1.5 m apart, buds to the sides, and cover with 5 cm of soil.
Keep moist and feed with nitrogen and potassium; earth up soil around the base as shoots grow to prevent lodging.
Harvest when the cane is mature (sweet tasting at the top as well as the base, 10–18 months), cutting close to the ground.
Crush canes to extract juice — drink fresh or boil down slowly into jaggery or syrup. New shoots (ratoons) regrow for 3–5 years.

lore: Alexander's admiral Nearchus reported Indian 'reeds that make honey without bees' in 325 BCE, and the word 'sugar' comes from Sanskrit 'śarkarā' via Persian and Arabic. Columbus carried cane to Hispaniola on his second voyage in 1493.
funFact: Sugarcane is the world's largest crop by harvested weight, about 1.9 billion tonnes a year.

summary: A trailing morning-glory relative from tropical America with sweet, starchy storage roots. Sweet potatoes reached Polynesia centuries before Columbus — widely taken as evidence of pre-Columbian contact between Polynesians and South Americans.
nativeRange: Tropical Central and northern South America; grown throughout the tropics and warm-temperate regions
abilities: Natural GM crop: its genome carries genes inserted by Agrobacterium thousands of years ago
Vines root at nodes, so a single plant can cover several square metres
Orange-fleshed types are very rich in β-carotene, used in Africa to fight vitamin A deficiency
Produces food in poor soils and survives typhoons that flatten grain crops
edibleParts: leaves and shoot tips (cooked, widely eaten in Africa and Asia)
edibilityNote: Roots and leaves are eaten cooked. Roots attacked by weevils or mould can contain toxic furanoterpenoids (e.g. ipomeamarone); cut away bitter, blemished parts.

uses.use: Roots to strengthen the spleen and ease constipation
White-skinned sweet potato ('caiapo') extract taken for diabetes, with small trials
Orange-fleshed sweet potato promoted to prevent vitamin A deficiency (World Food Prize 2016)

medicinal.cautions: Discard damaged, bitter roots. High oxalate in leaves.

fruit.description: Small, round, dry capsule about 5–8 mm, holding 1–4 seeds; flowers are lavender-to-white morning-glory trumpets.

seed.description: Hard, angular to rounded, dark-brown to black seeds about 3–4 mm, with a very tough coat
seed.dispersal: Gravity; vegetatively by humans; possibly ocean drift and birds
seed.germination: Breeding only: scarify (nick or acid) and sow at 25–30 °C. Gardeners use slips

grow.zones: Annual warm-season crop (USDA 4–11 with 90–150 frost-free days); perennial in tropics
grow.water: Moderate; drought-tolerant once established
grow.soil: Loose, sandy loam, well-drained, pH 5.5–6.5; avoid rich nitrogen soils (all leaves, few roots)
grow.propagation: Slips (rooted sprouts) or vine cuttings
grow.timeToHarvest: 90–150 days
steps: Grow slips by half-submerging a sweet potato in water or burying it in damp sand in a warm place; snap off sprouts at 15–20 cm and root them in water.
After frost, when soil is above 18 °C, plant slips 30–40 cm apart in raised ridges, burying them to the top leaves.
Water until established; avoid heavy nitrogen feeding.
Lift vines periodically so they don't root everywhere, and pick some tips for cooking.
Dig carefully before frost, when roots are a good size; cure in a warm (around 30 °C), humid place for 7–10 days to sweeten and heal skins, then store at 13–15 °C.

lore: Kūmara reached Polynesia by about 1000–1100 CE, and Māori grew it in New Zealand with elaborate rituals to the god Rongo. In Japan, the Edo scholar Aoki Konyō promoted the sweet potato as famine insurance in the 1730s, earning the nickname 'Kansho Sensei' (Master Sweet Potato).
funFact: The Polynesian word 'kūmara' closely resembles the Quechua 'kumar' — often cited as a clue that Polynesians reached South America, though linguists still debate the link.

summary: A climbing orchid from Mexican and Central American forests and the source of real vanilla, the second most expensive spice after saffron. Outside its homeland every flower must be hand-pollinated, a method invented in 1841 by Edmond Albius, a 12-year-old enslaved boy on Réunion.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico, Central America and northern South America; cultivated in Madagascar, Réunion, Indonesia, Uganda, Papua New Guinea and India
abilities: Climbs trees with aerial roots that cling to bark
Each flower opens for only a few hours on a single morning
A thin flap (rostellum) separates male and female parts, preventing self-pollination without help
Green pods have no flavour; vanillin develops only after weeks of curing
edibilityNote: Cured pods and extract are safe. The sap of fresh stems and green pods can cause skin irritation ('vanillism') in plantation workers.

uses.use: Vanilla mixed into remedies and amulets and taken with cacao as a tonic
Listed as a stimulant, digestive and aphrodisiac

medicinal.cautions: Contact dermatitis from fresh sap.

fruit.description: Slender, fleshy green pod 15–25 cm long that, when cured, turns supple, glossy, deep chocolate-brown and intensely aromatic, sometimes frosted with vanillin crystals.

seed.description: Tens of thousands of minute, round, glossy black seeds about 0.3 mm — the 'vanilla specks' in ice cream
seed.dispersal: Probably bees and other animals in the wild; seeds lack food reserves
