seed.germination: Needs symbiotic fungi or sterile lab culture; practically impossible at home. Cultivation is by cuttings

grow.water: High humidity; regular water, with a 2–3 month drier spell to trigger flowering
grow.soil: Loose, humus-rich mulch over well-drained soil (it roots mostly in leaf litter)
grow.propagation: Stem cuttings 1–2 m long with 6–12 nodes
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–4 years to first flowers; pods 8–9 months after pollination
steps: Plant a 1–2 m cutting at the base of a living support tree (e.g. Gliricidia, Jatropha) or a post, laying 2–3 leafless nodes on the soil and covering them with mulch.
Tie the vine to its support and keep it shaded and humid; mulch thickly with leaves.
Loop the vine back down when it reaches 1.5–2 m so flowers form within reach.
Each morning in the flowering season, hand-pollinate open flowers: lift the rostellum with a toothpick and press the anther onto the stigma.
Pick pods when the tip yellows; cure by scalding in 65 °C water, 'sweating' wrapped in blankets, then sunning by day and wrapping at night for weeks before slow drying.

lore: The Totonac people of Veracruz say vanilla sprang from the blood of a princess, Xanat, and her lover. Edmond Albius's thumb-and-stick technique (1841) made Réunion and Madagascar the centre of world vanilla, but he died in poverty.
funFact: Less than 1% of the vanilla flavour sold worldwide comes from real vanilla; the rest is synthetic vanillin.

summary: A woody climbing vine from the Western Ghats of Kerala whose dried berries are the world's most traded spice. Black, white, green and red peppercorns all come from the same plant, harvested and processed differently.
nativeRange: Western Ghats, south-west India (Malabar Coast); cultivated in Vietnam, Indonesia, Brazil, India, Sri Lanka and Malaysia
abilities: Climbs by roots at each node that grip tree bark
Pungency comes from piperine, which also increases absorption of curcumin and some drugs
Spikes of tiny flowers are self- and rain-pollinated
Vines produce for 20–30 years
edibleParts: dried berries (black, white, green, red peppercorns)
edibilityNote: Safe as a spice. Large amounts irritate the gut, and inhaled powder causes sneezing.

uses.use: One of the 'trikatu' (three pungents, with long pepper and ginger) to kindle digestive fire and clear mucus
Pepper for colds, coughs and as a digestive
Piperine added to curcumin supplements to raise bioavailability

medicinal.cautions: Piperine can raise blood levels of some drugs (e.g. phenytoin, propranolol) by inhibiting their metabolism.

fruit.season: Harvested 6–8 months after flowering, usually in the dry season
fruit.description: Long hanging spikes 7–15 cm carrying 50–150 small round drupes, green ripening to red.

seed.description: Each peppercorn is a single-seeded drupe about 4–6 mm; black pepper is the wrinkled, dried unripe fruit; white pepper is the smooth, cream-grey seed with the outer skin removed
seed.germination: Sow fresh ripe red berries (pulp removed) 1 cm deep at 25–30 °C in shade; slow and erratic, 3–6 weeks. Cuttings preferred

grow.water: High (2,000–3,000 mm rain), with good drainage
grow.soil: Rich, humus-laden, well-drained, pH 5.5–6.5
grow.propagation: Runner-shoot or stem cuttings of 2–3 nodes
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–4 years to first crop
steps: Root 2–3-node cuttings from runner shoots in shaded, moist potting mix.
Plant beside a living support tree (e.g. Erythrina, Gliricidia, coconut, areca) or a rough post 3–4 m tall, in partial shade.
Tie the vine to its support as it climbs; mulch heavily and feed with compost.
Keep soil moist but never waterlogged — wet roots invite foot rot (Phytophthora).
Pick whole spikes when 1–2 berries turn red; dry in the sun for 5–7 days until black and wrinkled, or soak ripe berries and rub off skins for white pepper.

lore: Peppercorns were stuffed in the nostrils of Ramesses II's mummy (died 1213 BCE). Alaric the Visigoth demanded 3,000 pounds of pepper as part of the ransom of Rome in 408 CE, and Vasco da Gama's 1498 arrival in Calicut was driven by the pepper trade.
funFact: In medieval Europe pepper was so valuable it was used to pay rent — the origin of the term 'peppercorn rent'.

summary: A small evergreen laurel of Sri Lanka whose inner bark, peeled and rolled into fragile quills, is 'true cinnamon'. Its trade was so lucrative that Arab middlemen spun tales of cinnamon guarded by giant birds to hide its origin. The wild species is assessed as Vulnerable.
nativeRange: Sri Lanka and the southern Western Ghats of India; cultivated in Sri Lanka, Madagascar, the Seychelles and elsewhere
abilities: Inner bark curls naturally into quills as it dries
Coppiced stools regrow new shoots for harvest every 2 years for decades
Contains far less coumarin than cassia cinnamon (C. cassia)
Young leaves flush bright red before turning green
edibilityNote: Safe as a spice. Concentrated essential oil irritates skin and mucous membranes; cassia (often sold as cinnamon) is high in coumarin, which can harm the liver in large regular doses.

uses.use: Tvak (bark) for colds, indigestion and to balance kapha
Cinnamon bark (ròu guì, mainly cassia) to warm the body and kidneys
Used in embalming and kyphi incense

medicinal.cautions: Cinnamon oil is a strong irritant and sensitiser; supplements may lower blood sugar.

fruit.season: Ripens about 6 months after flowering (often June–August)
fruit.description: Small, oval, dark-purple to black drupe 1–1.5 cm, sitting in a cup-like persistent calyx.

seed.description: A single oval, smooth seed 8–10 mm, pale brown to dark brown, inside the thin black flesh
seed.germination: Recalcitrant: clean and sow fresh, 1 cm deep, in warm shade at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 2–4 weeks

grow.water: High (1,500–2,500 mm rain)
grow.soil: Sandy, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; the famous Negombo cinnamon grows on white sand
grow.propagation: Seed or semi-hardwood cuttings; air layering
grow.timeToHarvest: First cut 2–3 years after planting; then every 1–2 years
steps: Sow fresh seed or root cuttings and plant out in sandy, well-drained soil 1–1.5 m apart.
After 2–3 years, coppice the plant to 10–15 cm above the ground to make it sprout many straight shoots.
Cut shoots 1.5–2.5 cm thick in the rainy season, when the bark peels easily.
Scrape off the outer bark, rub the stem with a brass rod to loosen the inner bark, slit and peel it in long strips.
Nest smaller strips inside larger ones to form quills; dry in shade for 4–5 days, then in sun.

lore: Herodotus reported that Arabians gathered cinnamon from the nests of giant birds, and Nero is said to have burned a year's supply of Rome's cinnamon at the funeral of his wife Poppaea. Portuguese and then Dutch control of Ceylon's cinnamon was fought over for two centuries.
funFact: The Dutch burned stocks of cinnamon in Amsterdam to keep prices high, and cultivated it on plantations only from the 1760s.

summary: An evergreen tree endemic to the tiny Banda Islands of Indonesia that yields two spices: nutmeg, the seed, and mace, its scarlet lace-like aril. The Dutch East India Company massacred and enslaved the Bandanese in 1621 to seize the monopoly.
nativeRange: Banda Islands, Maluku, Indonesia; cultivated in Indonesia, Grenada, India and Sri Lanka
abilities: Produces two different spices from one fruit — the seed (nutmeg) and the aril (mace)
Dioecious: about half of seedlings are male and fruitless
Myristicin and elemicin in the seed are psychoactive and toxic in large doses
Trees can fruit for 60 years or more
edibleParts: fruit flesh (candied, jams, Indonesian manisan pala)
edibilityNote: Safe as a spice in culinary amounts. Eating about 5 g or more (one or two whole nuts) can cause nutmeg poisoning: nausea, palpitations, hallucinations and delirium lasting a day or more.

uses.use: Jaiphal in small amounts for diarrhoea, insomnia and as a digestive
Nutmeg for stomach complaints and as an aphrodisiac
Carried in pomanders against plague

medicinal.cautions: Toxic and psychoactive in doses above about 5 g; dangerous in pregnancy and for children.

fruit.description: Pale-yellow, apricot-like fruit 5–8 cm that splits in two when ripe, revealing a glossy brown seed wrapped in a crimson, net-like aril.

seed.description: Egg-shaped, hard brown seed 2–3 cm with a dark, glossy, ridged shell; inside, the kernel (nutmeg) is grey-brown with cream marbling; when fresh it is wrapped in bright scarlet branching mace
seed.dispersal: Fruit pigeons (Ducula) swallow the seeds with their aril
seed.germination: Recalcitrant: sow fresh, in shell, 2 cm deep in shade at 25–30 °C; slow, 4–8 weeks

grow.sun: Partial shade when young; sun when mature
grow.water: High (over 2,000 mm rain)
grow.soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained volcanic or loamy soil, pH 6–7
grow.propagation: Seed (then select females), or grafting/approach-grafting female scions
grow.timeToHarvest: 5–8 years from seed; full crops after 15–20 years
steps: Sow fresh seeds in shaded nursery beds; plant out at 1–2 years, or plant grafted female trees to avoid fruitless males.
Space trees about 9 m apart under light shade (e.g. bananas or coconuts), with one male per 10 females.
Mulch thickly and keep moist; protect from strong winds.
Collect fruit when it splits open; separate the mace from the seed by hand.
Dry mace flat in the sun for a few days; dry seeds in the shell for 6–8 weeks until the kernel rattles, then crack and store.

lore: Under the 1667 Treaty of Breda, England and the Netherlands each kept what they had seized: the Dutch kept Run, a tiny nutmeg island in the Bandas, and the English kept New Amsterdam — Manhattan. Nutmeg remains so central to Grenada that it appears on the national flag.
funFact: Grenada's flag shows a nutmeg pod — the only national flag with a spice on it.

summary: Cloves are the unopened flower buds of an evergreen myrtle from the North Moluccas, the original 'Spice Islands'. Cloves were found in a kitchen at Terqa, Syria, dated to about 1720 BCE — evidence of a spice trade spanning 8,000 km nearly 4,000 years ago.
nativeRange: North Maluku, Indonesia (Ternate, Tidore, Moti, Makian, Bacan); cultivated in Indonesia, Zanzibar and Pemba, Madagascar and Sri Lanka
abilities: Buds contain up to 15–20% essential oil, mostly eugenol
Eugenol is a natural anaesthetic and antiseptic
Trees can crop for over a century
Afo, a clove tree on Ternate, is reputed to be over 350 years old
edibilityNote: Safe as a spice. Undiluted clove oil can burn the mouth and gums, and swallowed oil has caused serious liver damage and seizures in young children.

uses.use: Lavanga for toothache, bad breath, cough and indigestion
Eugenol mixed with zinc oxide as a temporary filling and dressing for dry socket
Officials held cloves in their mouths to sweeten their breath before addressing the emperor

medicinal.cautions: Undiluted oil is caustic; oil is dangerous to children if swallowed; eugenol may increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants.

fruit.season: Buds harvested twice a year in many regions; fruits rarely allowed to form
fruit.description: If left, buds open into fluffy crimson-stamened flowers and then purple-red oval berries ('mother of cloves') about 2.5 cm long.

seed.description: The dried spice is a nail-shaped bud 1–2 cm long, reddish-brown, with a ball-like head of petals. The true seed is one oblong, soft, pale-brown seed about 1.5 cm inside the purple berry
seed.germination: Recalcitrant: sow fresh ripe berries in shade at 25–30 °C; 2–5 weeks

grow.sun: Partial shade when young; sun when mature
grow.water: High (1,500–2,500 mm), with a short dry season for flowering
grow.soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained loam or volcanic soil, pH 5–6.5
grow.propagation: Seed
grow.timeToHarvest: 5–7 years to first buds; peak at 15–20 years
steps: Sow fresh seeds from ripe berries in a shaded nursery; transplant at 1–2 years.
Plant out about 6–8 m apart with temporary shade such as bananas; protect from wind.
Mulch and water regularly in the first years; weed around the base.
Pick bud clusters by hand when the buds turn from green to pink but before they open.
Separate buds from stems and sun-dry for 4–5 days until dark brown and they snap cleanly.

lore: Magellan's 1519–22 expedition sailed largely to reach the clove islands of Maluku, and the one surviving ship, Victoria, returned with 26 tonnes of cloves. Omani Sultan Said bin Sultan made Zanzibar the world's leading clove producer in the 19th century, using enslaved labour.
funFact: The word 'clove' comes from Latin clavus, 'nail', after the bud's shape — the same image behind the Chinese name 'nail spice'.

summary: A large, paddle-jointed cactus domesticated in central Mexico, cultivated for its sweet fruit (tunas) and tender young pads (nopales). It also hosts the cochineal insect, source of the brilliant carmine red that dyed European royalty's robes and still colours food.
nativeRange: Domesticated in central Mexico; naturalised throughout the Mediterranean, North and East Africa, the Middle East, India and Australia
abilities: CAM photosynthesis lets it fix carbon at night, using up to 5 times less water than grain crops
Any pad that touches soil can root into a new plant
Hosts cochineal scale insects, whose carminic acid gives carmine dye
Prickly pears became notorious weeds in Australia (mainly O. stricta), famously cleared by the Cactoblastis moth; O. ficus-indica itself is invasive in South Africa
edibilityNote: Fruit and young pads are eaten. Remove the tiny barbed hair-like spines (glochids) carefully — they lodge in skin and mouth. Eating very many seeds can cause intestinal blockage.

uses.use: Nopal pads eaten to lower blood sugar in diabetes, with small clinical studies showing reduced post-meal glucose
Flowers as a tea for kidney stones and diarrhoea

medicinal.cautions: May add to the effect of diabetes medication; glochids cause skin irritation.

fruit.description: Barrel- or egg-shaped berry 5–10 cm, green, yellow, orange, red or purple, studded with tufts of tiny spines; juicy, sweet, melon-like flesh of the same colour, full of seeds.

seed.description: Hard, flattened, round to kidney-shaped seeds 3–5 mm, beige to light brown, with a thick woody coat; 100–300 per fruit
seed.germination: Slow; scarify and sow at 25–30 °C in gritty mix; 2–8 weeks. Pads are the usual propagation

grow.water: Very low
grow.soil: Sandy, rocky, very well-drained; tolerates poor and alkaline soils
grow.propagation: Single pads (cladodes)
grow.timeToHarvest: 2–3 years from a planted pad
steps: Cut a healthy pad with tongs or thick gloves and let the cut end dry for 1–2 weeks until calloused.
Plant it upright, one-third buried, in dry, gritty soil in full sun; do not water for the first 2–3 weeks.
Water occasionally in the first summer; established plants need almost none.
Harvest young pads (nopalitos) in spring when 15–20 cm long, and scrape off spines before cooking.
Pick fruit with tongs when fully coloured, roll it in sand or burn off the glochids, then slice off the ends and peel.

lore: The Aztec founding legend says their wandering people would build their city where they saw an eagle perched on a nopal cactus — the image on Mexico's flag and the origin of Tenochtitlan. In Israel 'sabra', the prickly pear, is the nickname for native-born Israelis: prickly outside, sweet inside.
funFact: Carmine from cochineal insects on prickly pear was Spain's second most valuable export from the Americas after silver.

summary: A colossal, swollen-trunked tree of the African savanna that stores thousands of litres of water in its spongy wood and lives for over 2,000 years. Its velvety pods hold a dry, tangy, vitamin-C-rich powdery pulp eaten across the continent.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa from Senegal to Sudan, Ethiopia and south to South Africa; also the Arabian Peninsula; introduced in India, Madagascar and the Caribbean
abilities: Trunks store water and swell in the wet season; elephants gouge them for moisture
The oldest dated individual, Panke in Zimbabwe, was about 2,500 years old when it died in 2011
Large white flowers open at night and are pollinated by fruit bats
Bark regrows after stripping, so it can be harvested for fibre repeatedly
edibleParts: young leaves (fresh or dried as 'lalo' or 'kuka' soup thickener)
edibilityNote: Pulp, leaves and roasted seeds are widely eaten. Raw seeds contain antinutrients and are usually roasted or fermented.

uses.use: Fruit pulp mixed with water for diarrhoea and fever; leaves for kidney and bladder ailments
Bark decoction used as a substitute for quinine against fever

medicinal.cautions: Seed oil contains cyclopropenoid fatty acids; usually refined before use.

fruit.season: Dry season (pods ripen months after the wet-season flowering)
fruit.description: Hanging, oval to oblong pod 15–25 cm with a hard, velvety greenish-grey to brown shell; inside, chalky cream-white pulp in dry chunks around seeds and reddish fibres.

seed.description: Hard, kidney-shaped, dark brown to black seeds about 1–1.5 cm, embedded in powdery white pulp
seed.dispersal: Baboons, elephants and other mammals; also water
seed.germination: Very hard coat: soak in hot water or nick, then soak 24 hours; sow at 25–30 °C; 1–4 weeks

grow.water: Low; intolerant of waterlogging
grow.soil: Sandy or rocky, very well-drained, pH 6–8
grow.propagation: Seed; grafting for earlier fruiting
grow.timeToHarvest: 8–23 years from seed; grafted trees in as little as 4–5 years
steps: Scarify seeds, soak, and sow in deep pots to accommodate the taproot.
Plant out in full sun in deep, free-draining soil, with lots of space — trunks can reach 10 m across.
Water young trees only in the dry season; protect from goats and cattle.
Harvest young leaves for cooking regularly without harming the tree; in bonsai or pots, keep dry in winter.
Gather fallen ripe pods, crack the shell and sieve the dry pulp to separate seeds and fibres.

lore: In many African traditions the baobab was planted upside down by a god, its roots in the air, and in Senegal griots were once buried inside hollow baobab trunks. Hollow baobabs have served as stores, shelters and even a prison near Derby in Western Australia (the related boab).
funFact: Between 2005 and 2017, nine of the 13 oldest known African baobabs died or lost their oldest parts, a collapse scientists suspect is linked to climate change.
